THE latest verbal atrocity is " funeralise." It ehould be applied at once to any person who ventures to use it. AN old bachelor wants to know if you ever sat down to tea„when- skimmed milk was on the table, without being asked, "Do you take cream ?" Buss—to kiss. Sillybus—to kiss the hand instead of the lips. Erebus—to kiss in the dark. Blunder- bus—to kiss the wroug, person. Omnibus—kisses all round.- - "SAM," said it master to a sleepy-headed ap- prentice, "have you ever seen a snail?" "Yes, sir." "Then you must have met it, for you never could have overtaken SAID Bobby to the minister at dinner—" Can a church whistle?" "Why do you ask ? " "Cos pa owes £2 back pew rent, and he says he's going to let the church whistle for it."

Miss CLAW.: Are you familiar .with the works of George Eliot, Mr. Featherly ? Mr. Featherly : , Well-er, yes. I used to be, but I haven't read any- ' thing from his pen. since I was a boy.* THE newspaper correspondent who signs himself " One Who Knows" is generally the one who knows the least about the matter—which fact he , makes apparent in his communication. PROzESSIONAL pedestrian: "Hello, Tommy, how's business ? " Amateur tramp: "Looking up." Professional pedestrian: "How's that ? " Amateur tramp: "Why, it's so flat on its back it can't do anything else. " THERE 1" said the exasperated editor, as the sylphlike form of the persistent poet shot up from the toe of his patent leather and was gently wafted over the sill of the office door; "that's what I call a rising poet." "I DECLARE, Charley," exclaimed Clara, "you take the words right out of my mouth 1" "Oh, mamma," piped in the little pitcher, "now I know. what Clara and Charley were doing out in the hall when she let him in!"

"WHAT do they do when they install a minister?" inquired a small boy. "Do they put him in a stall and feed him ?" "Not a bit," said the father; "they harness him to the church and expect him to draw it alone." _ _

AT a negro wedding, when the minister read the words, "love, hnnour, and obey," the groom inter- rupted him and said, "Read that agin, sah read it waned mo', so's de lady kin ketch de full solemn- ity of de meaning. I'se been married befo." "DID not the sight of the boundless blue sea, bearing on Its bosom the white winged fleets of c,ommeroe, fill you with emotion ?" "Yes," replied the traveller, "for a while it did, blip after a while it didn't fill me with anything. It sorter emptied me." "WHO is that man applauding so vociferously near the front ?' asked a friend of a theatrical manager on the first production of a play in a pro- vincial theatre. "That long-haired man with a light-coloured coat?" "Yes," "He—he's the author of the play." "Thi sorry to hear, Mrs. Brown," said the minister, "that you were present last night at a Plymouth Brethren's tea meeting. I have often told you that these doctrines are highly erroneous." Mrs. Brown— " Well, sir, their doctrines may be, but their cake with sultana raisins is excellent."

"ONE word more," said a speaker, "and ram done." And the reporters found, when the word was written down, that it contained fifteen hundred syllable. The famous word of Aristophanes was outdone. The same speaker is the fellow who often says "a single remark," and then talks for fifteen minutes.

OVERHEARD Coming out of church She,: "Next time you want to sleep during the sermon you'd better go and sit with. Mr. A., and lay your head on him. You'd be really comfortable then." He: " Why ? Is Mr. A. nice and -- ahem soft ? " She: "No; but he's one of the pillars of the church."

JOHNNY laboriously lugged a pail into the parlour, where the family were assembled, and asked his maternal grandmother to kick it. "Why should I kick it, Johnny?" grandmother inquired in amaze- ment. "Just to amuse papa," said Johnny. "He said ke would give five pounds any time to see you kick the bucket."

A GENTLEMAN saw a person poring over an atlas and seemingly disconcerted by want of success. "Can't you find what you want 7 " he inquired, "or can I assist you?" "I don't know," was the reply —" for I have been looking for two hours thfough all latitudes, and cannot discover this Liliput any- where."

A LITTLE fellow, who was at a neighbour's house about noon the other day, watched the preparations for dinner with great interest, but when asked to stay and eat something he promptly refused. "Why, yes, Johnnie, you had better stay," said the lady. "I can't." "Why can't you ? " "Well, 'cause," said the little fellow, "mamma said r mustn't unless you ask me three times." They in- vited him twice more right off. A GENTLEMAN goes to an armourer's and asks for a revolver, "Here's a real nice family weapon," says the clerk. "Family weapon?" "Yes, family weapon? just the thing for domestic tragedies; six-shooter, you see, sir—two bullets for your wife, two bullets for the destroyer of your happiness, twe for yourself. All the go, sir! Sell hundreds of 'em for bridal presents, sir." GOOD MINISTER—" If is rather odd that the col- lections are exactly one dollar less than they used to be." Minister's Wife—" Nothing odd about it." "We have not lost any of our congregation." No; but I suppose that you remember that Mr. Pious never used to give less than a dollar." "Of course." "Well, Mr. Pious has been elected a deacon, and he passes the plate now."—Omaha World. TILE late Lord Kelly, who was remakable for his rubicundity of nose, having spoken rather disre- spectfully of a gentleman in the army, an Irishman present observed that if any man that had lived, or ever had lived, or ever could live, had said the same of him, he would have pulled him by the nose. "Yes," replied Foote, "I dare say you would; but in the present case that would not do; there are ways enough of revenging an insult without running one's head into the fire."

DOMINIC°, the favourite buffoon of Louis XIV., being one evening admitted to the presence of the Bing during supper, said not a word, nor uttered the least remark, but seemed wholly absorbed in the contemplation of a dish of partridges of an exquisite appearance. The King perceiving what it was that so closely engaged his attention, and wishing to make him talk, said, " e that dish to Dominico." "And the partridges, too, sire ?" "And the partridges, too," replied the magnificent monarch, pleased with his wit. The dish was gold. Sin PATRICK BLAKE was once in company where a nobleman was relating many wonderful accounts of echoes which he had heard abroad, more particu- larly one in the ruins of a temple on the Appian Way, about twelve miles from Rome, which, he said, "repeated any words seventy times." "That, replied Sir Patrick, "is nothing wonderful. There is an echo on my brother's estate, near the Lake of Kilarney, in Ireland, to which I 'have frequently said, 4 Goodmorrow, Madam Echo,' and I was im- mediately answered, 'Good-morrow, Sir Patrick Blake; how do you do T" Two mammas were the other evening exchang- ing confidences at a ball. The topic came to be the recent marriage of Mrs. A.'s daughtF. "Well, my dear Mrs. A.," said Mrs. 8., "I must say that your dear Ethel's marriage with that man astonished us all," "Yes," sighed Mrs. A., in return, "it was a great mistake, I must admit. But who could have imagined that the brute would have no money? Between you and me, my dear, he was such an utter wreck as to his health, he was so an ugly, so stupid, and so badly bred that we all of us felt convinced he must be rolling in wealth." IT is related that one of the little Archduchesses of Austria was taken to a circus, where nothing amazed her and very little pleased her. On her return home the Emperor asked how she had enjoyed the performance. "Oh, very well," the young lady replied, "only mamma does everything the circus-women did a great deal better. Why, I have seen her jump through six hoops." It appears that this is really true, and that the Empress has on more than one occasion given a strictly private entertainment to her intimates, in which she has surprised them with feats equal to those of the most skilled circus-riders..

div.head: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.

Like her eldest daughter, Mrs. Cornwallis, WeA was married at seventeen. She watt Miss Mary- Fitzgerald, daughter of the Rev. Frederick Fitz- gerald, rector of Cloone, Leitrim. She atrried Mr. Cornwallis West in 1872, and has two daughters and a son..

Mr. Magee, who has been elected without opr,o- sition President of the Oxford Union, is a Speaker of some promise. He is the son of the late Arch- bishop, and inherits many of his good qualities. Very vehement in speech, he ekes out the smallness of his person with much and richly varied gesticu- lntion. He has his full share of humor, arpd—which is still more important in a debating society—good humor.

Prince Henry of Pless and his bride threw off all ceremony on Tuesday when they emerged from the church doors made one. in the evening they drove up to Charing-cross alone, and walked up and down the platform, into &Viers and. Pond's buffet, into the Charing-cross Hotel and out again, bought papers and Christmas numbers by the score, and altogether behaved like a staid married couple of long standing. They left by the 5.35 for Folke- stone en route for the Riviera.

Commander Cameron has for the last few months been spending a good deal of his time in Brussels. As a result he is now appointed one of the tWo new administrators of the Kadtanga Company, and will, we, believe, soon leave for Africa. The gallant officor, the first Englishman to cross the Dark Con- tinent on foot, is short, wiry; " bearded like the pard," and possessed of a pair of marVellously flash- ing eyes. In his dealings with the natives he always avoids the " stringent " methods populat with some explorers.

The illness of the Duke of Devonshire reminds us that he is one of the few surviving members of an unreformed House of Commons. He sat for Mahon in 1831—the year previous to the first Reform Act. In Ireland likewise there still survicus a legislator of the pre-Reform .period. Mr. O'Neill Daunt, of Kilcarson Abbey, co. Cork, was private R•ecretary to O'Connell, and was member for Mallow, in 1831. Mr. Daunt, who is now in his eighty-fifth year, is is full intellectual vigor, and has quite recently con- tributed articles to the" Westminster Review.

Russell Sage, the New York millionaire, who had such a marvellous escape the other day, while, one of the richest men in America, is one of the most 'close-fisted." It is a boast that for years his lunch has never cost him over 2id., and he will cling to an old hat with a vigor that exceeds that with which Burns clung to the Straw Hat of the Dock Strike. Mrs. Sage, however, insists upon distribut- ing a large amount in charity. Mr. Sage is one of the pillars of the Presbyterian Church in Nevi York city, and a social as well as financial leading citizen.

Condolences to Mr. D'Oyly Cate upon the death of his father, who has died at Reigate at the age of eighty-fbur. Mr. Richard Carte was at one time 'a well-known performer on -the flute, and became later in life a partner in a firm of musical instru- 'nielit makers. Mr. D'Oyly Carte, who is the eldest son of his father, for'years worked (and played) in :the smile manner. The first ° ekperinient in theatrical management attempted in London by the founder of the Royal English Opera House was madelat the Royalty Theatre a generation ago, whed Mr. D'Oyly Carte dabbled in French comic Opera.

The death of the Emperor of Brazil recalls one of the many romantic incidents in the life of Mr. Jas. O'Kelly, M.P., for North Roscommon, who accom- panied the Emperor some years ago in his voyage from Rio Janeiro and his tour through the United States. The Emperor and Empress of Brazil were on deck in Somewhat stormy weather. Mr. Q'Kelly who was in their company at the time, observed a spar falling straight on the head of the Empress.'l With great presence of mind he placed his arm be- tween the spar and the Empress and thus, at the cost,to himself of a broken arm, chivalrously warded off alblow which would have been fatal to her Majesty.

Mrs. Parnell—the mother of the late Mr. Parnell —who has just embarked at New 'York for Europe, is a tall portly old lady, who bears the weight of seventy years lightly. She is truly striking in ap- pearance. She has clear blue eyes, Roman nose, broad forehead, and finely chiselled mouth. She dresses with great simplicity and elegance, and very old and costly laceis generally a feature in her at- tire. Mrs. Parnell, although an American by birth —she is the daughter of an admiral in the American navy—speaks with a perfect English accent, and in the slow distinct tones affected by the upper ten. She is very well informed and has a remarkably tenacious memory.

The visit Mr. Gladstone is paying to Earl Spencer at Althorpe is his second sojourn at the Red Earl's beautiful Northamptonshire seat. tie was there about twelve years ago, and then spent nearly the whole of his time revelling in the great library— the largest private collection of books in the world. There was, during his stay, a meet Of the Pytchley Hounds upon the lawn in.front of the mansion. A meet of the pink-coated: white-collared-followers of the historic Midland pack is always picturesque, and the meet on this occasion was particularly large. Mr. Gladstone came out and looked at it for a few moments, but he seemed out of his element, and soon shuffled off btick to the library.

John Austin, fisherman, of Sittingbourne, was in the local bankruptcy court, the other day ;with lia- bilities scheduled at £l5 78. 6d. He attributed his insolvency to the bargemen's strike. He had a little shop in the town, but his earnings only ranged from 16s. to XI a week. He offered 68. in the pound by instalments of CI. a month. The judge, however, would not hear of such a proposition, and insisted that the debtor should pay nothing less than 128. in the pound at the rate of 4s. a fortnight. Doubtless, John Austin has seen the moral of this case, which is written big enorgh. If you must fail, let it be not for £l5 but £15,000, and don't let your offer be more than 2d. in the pound or thereabouts. Things will go smoothly enough then.

The election of Representative Crisp, of Georgia, to be,Speaker of the United States House of Repre- sentatives, places in the chair a man born in Eng- land, and no doubt some facetious member will ex- claim,"! know that man: he comes from Sheffield," for it was in that city, while his parents were visit- ing friends, the new Speaker first saw the light, in the year 1845. It is rather a strange coincidence that aman born on English soil should be the pre- siding officer of an American legislative body, con- trolled by a party in which the Irish people are chiefly found. Mr. Crisp fought on the Confederate side during the Civil War, and was a prisoner in one of the Northern forts for nearly two years. He was a judge of his own State and has been in Con- gress eight years.

The "Times "correspondent at Calcutta, takes the trouble to telegrapk to London that the Madras papers are "gratified" at the Viceroy having pub- licly complimented Lord Wenlock on his devoted services in the famine-stricken districts. What an easy thing it is to get a gratuitous puff if you hap- pen to be a peer, holding a post worth Its. 10,000 a 3 ear! First Lord Lansdowne butters Lord Wenlock. Then the Madras Press butters Lord Lansdowne for buttering Lord Wenlock. Then the" Times" but- ters the Madras Press for buttering the Viceroy for buttering Lord Wenlock. It is La beautiful and touching sight, but it takes the gilt off the ginger- bread to remember that this flummery is the best answer that can be given to Mr. Caine's damming accusations against Lord Wenlock's administra- tion.

One of the most idiotic phases of the poor law was illustrated a few days ago at Horncastle. A middle-aged man, married, was summoned for fail- ing .to comply with an order to pay one shilling week to the Horncastle Guardians tor the support of his father. The man showed that he was only in casual employment, earning about 10s. a week. He had been ill, and was permanently incapacitated to some extent by an injury to his ankle. The magis- trates adjourned the case, ordering him to pay the costs. It then transpired that the man had only 3d. in his pocket, and that he had walked forty- three miles to attend the court in answer to the summons, and was completely overcome by fatigue. This seems to have touched even the hearts of the Horncastle bench, and they mercifully ordered the man to be allowed to start on his forty-three miles walk home. A pretty monument he: must have been, when he got home, of the ,tender mercies of the "guardians of the poor !"

" EAWR 808 AN' Mil'

" Two yungSters, upo' fun intent, Geet ready, an' to Lunnon went;' An' wo d'yo think thay wur, that's meant? Eawr Bob an' Me! -Two greenish jokers ther's no deawt, But th' Cockneys very soon fund eawt, •We wern't lung knowin' th' way ateawt— • Eawr Bob an' Me.! We went i' lodgin's wi' a Jew, An' when he tried uz chaps to "do," We towt kim just a thing or two— Eawr Bob an' Mel We uset to strowl abeawt at neets, Up coorts an' alleys, lones an' streets; An' eh! BY.9'yow ! we see'd stoiseets Eawr Bob an' Me!

Ther wuzn't one aleheause fth' teawn, But wot we had it jotted deawn, Fro' Dirty,Diek's to th' Rose an' Creawn— Eawr Bob an' Mel One neet.ii Bobby moved us,on, For singin', after 12 had, "John Wesley wur a good owd mon ! " Eawr Bob an' Me.

Another neet, Lincoln's Inn, • We shud ha' bin mixt up wi sin, But we wur not so flush o" tin " Eawr Bob an' Me. Another time at Crib we play'd, But, sumheaw, th' cards like pigeons stray'd, An' uz pured eawt afore we'd paid— Eawr Bob An' Me.

The Derby, top. we went to see, An' Jemmy Merry up a tree, Wen Kettledrum broke lawn Dundee, An' Bob an' Me! We seet Off once to Hampton Coort, To hey a day o' gradely spoort, But just that once we geet wool floor't— Eawr Bob an' Me! But don't mistake, we wern't aw bad, Nor played sich tricks ez made uz sad' Wile sumtimes th' Parson made uz glad— Eawr Bob an' Me. The, Parson !—eh, but lads, howd on! Tho, thirty year hez welly gone, Wen' not fergetten that owd Mon— Eawr Bob an' Me
Sum other time, if yo7ll insert it, . An' aw con get my oisni quill startet, , Aw'll tell you heaw we geet convertet— • Eawr Bob an' Me TUM 0' PEGS.
Nyowten, December, 1891.
LEATHER TRADES DEMONSTRATION AT WARRINGTON.

On Saturday afternoon, a demonstration was held at Warrington, in connection with the Amal- gamated Leather Trades Union, and the Warring- ton Trades and Labour Council. A piocession,num- bering at least 150 persons, started about three o'clock,from the Seven Stars Inn,and, headed by St. Paul's band, paraded the following streets :—St. James's-street, Knutsford-road, to the "Cheshire Cheese fl—back by the same route to Mersey-street, Church-street, School' Brow, 'Fennell-street, Dial- street, Buttermermarket-street, Scotiand-rd., Horse- market-street, Sankey-street, Bank Quay Bridge, Priestly-st., Froghall-lane, Tanner's-lane to Town's .End, The silk banner belonging to the Union and brought from London by Mr. H. Preece, the general secretary, and upon which appears representa- tions of the Bermondsey Leather Exchange, and of tan yard operations; was a conspicuous feature in the procession; and there were other banners bearing ,such mottoes as "Simon the tanner," "The Leather Trade Union," "'There's nothing like leather," and " Unity is strength." The unionists in the evening held an outdoor meeting in frdnt of the Rodney Hotel. Mr. W.. Bullock, secretary of :the* Warrington Trades Council,presiding. The CHAIRMAN having made a few remarks, Mr. T. MALKIN, delegate tb" the Trades' Council, ad- dressed those present. He referred to the number of women there, and said he mould like to see them or- ganised as Unionists, because if they became such they would imbue their children with the principles of Unionism. Women in the Black Country, from which he came, had achieved grea t triumphs by combination. The tanners of Warrington, he said, had to congratulate themsalves on a Trades Union victory that had been won there. The wealth, he said, at present all rested , in the hands of a few capitalists; and it was necessary that the working-men should organise, so that they might enjoy some of the wealth which they created.. .

Mr. Join-4 PRICE, district secretary of the Navvies', Bricklayers', and General Labourers' Union, was the succeeding speaker. That meeting, he said, wag a meet- ing in favour of the working-men of this country being better paid for their labour, and having less slavery ,and more enjoyment.of life. It was uo use their drudg- ging all the way along. They wanted a little easier times : it would take alot of easy work to kill him. The "bosses" had all easy work. Those present were not there to say that because they had won in a certain dispute they were to be idle as Unionists for the future., They were there to proclaim that, Trades Unionism meant brotherly feeling among men; and also that when the time came they were prepared to stand like men, shoulder to shoulder, but they had not ,come there to defy anybody.' 'They did not bid defiance to employers, but they must be determined to work for nothing less than would maintain them in a proper position ; and the only way to get this was to join a Trades Union.

Mr. A. E. BENJAMIN, a non-unionist, then spoke, de- claring himself heart and soul with the unionists. Work- ingmen had been too long subjected to the screw of capitalists, and they were there to say whether they would endure it any longer. Labour was before capital, and had a right ta stand in its proper position before capital now. It was time they demanded their liberty and asserted their right to the goods and luxuries of this world in equal measure with their employers. Mr. PREECE was the next speaker: lie said the Leather Trades Union of Warrington, assisted by the local Trades Council, had done something to maintain the standard of wages, and to obtain the conditions of manhood. (A. voice: " A lie.") During the last 30 years every industry in the countri had derived like advantages from carrying out the principle of combina- tion.

Mr. R. STOREY afterwards spoke. Nothing but thorough combination, he said, would enable workers to maintain their position, and there was no trade that more demanded advance of wages and better conditions than the leather trade.
The CHAIRMAN then dissolved the meeting, and about 75 of the unionists subsequently partook of tea at Mr. J. Price's Central Temperance Hotel in Winwick-street.
MR. THOMAS SN APE AT HEYWOOD.

On Saturday evening the annual soiree of the Hey- wood Reform Club was held in the large Assembly room of the club. Afterwards a meeting was held, at which there was a large attendance. Alderman Isherwood J.P., presided, supported by Mr. T. D. Sullivan, M.P. Mr. Thomas Snape, of Widnes, Liberal candidate for the Heywood division, said the recent speeches delivered by the Tory leaders showed that they were in a state of alarm at the Liberal victories at by-elections. It was obvious that the Conservative party was at sixes and sevens. Either there would be no Irish Bill at all, or it would be a phantom Bill that had been whittled down until its provisions were of such a milk-and-water char- acter as to be of no service to anybody, and therefore of no value. (Cheers.) Dealing with Mr. Goschen's speeches and letters in defence of his finance, Mr. Snape said there was a French proverb which said that when a man excused himself he accused himself, and that seemed to be the identical position in which Mr. Goschen found himself. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. Goschen had for the first time given the House of Lords control ckver the public purse, and that was a most pernicious principle to be introduced. A Bill had been passed for the expenditure of £21,000,000 on armaments, this sum to be extended o'er the next four years. It was one of the principles of the Constitution that no Act of Parlia- ment can be repealed except by consent 4 both Houses of Parliament, and if the Liberals on comiiig into power should think it wise to discontinue this extravagance they would have to pass another Bill which would have to go to the House of Lords, and the Lords would thus for a time have the power to regulate the expenditure of the country. Mat was a most pernicious principle to be introduced. (Loud cheers.)

CHRISTMAS BOOKS, Sze.

"The Fatal Request" is the title of a novel by M. A. L. Harris, author of "Mine own familiar friend.'" ,The plot is an unusual one, involving what on the face of it seems to be an unusually cold-blooded murder; and it is most elaborately and ingeneously :worked out.. There is, perhaps, too nitwit of detail 'here end there, but, on the whole, the interest is well sustained: The characters are clearly defined, and the ending is very satisfactory. The novel, which is one of some 400 pages is published by Messrs. F. Warne and Co., price 28. "The same firm are issuing a sixpenny edition, of over 200 pages' of "The Caxtons," by Sir Edward Bulwer Lytton. The type and paper are good; there is a neat coloured cover; and the issue ought there- fore to have a large sale. " 'The'Little Merrymakers" is a charming Christmas publication by Messrs. F. Warne and 00., the text being by A. J., Daryl!, and the illustrations from the prolific and artistic pencil of Constance Hazlewood. The chrome and other plates are beautifully executed, and the verse is considerably above the average. "The Century" for December has sundry Christmas features, including a poem on "The Christ Child," and a drawing of the Holy Family, by Frank Vincent Dumond. Raphael is dealt with under "Italian Old Masters," with several full;page reproductions of his most famous pictures. Amongst other illustrated papers we have " Mozart—after 100 years ;" "The Bowery "Ocean from real life;" and "The golden age of Pagel." There are the usual open letters, and light verse, under the head of" In lighter vein." . No better Christmas book for young people can be had than " Tales from Wonderland,' published (price is.) by Mr. Walter Scott, in the Camelot series. These stories are from the pen of Rudolph Baumba,ch, who is possessed of fertility of invention, and great delicacy and humour. The volume is well calculated to please both old and young. In the same series we have the "Life of Miguel de Cervantes." Itis written by Mr. H. E. Watts, Who has spared no time or pains to get at all that has been known about the author of" Don Quixote," and it must be said that he has presented his matter in the most read- able style. Byron says that" Cervantes smiled Spain's chivalry away." Whether this be so or not the story may be classed amongst the immortals, and the author's adventurous life is almost as interesting as the story Itself. ' A little volume which will charm cultured readers is "The Golden Treasury of. the best songs and lyrical poems in the English language, selected and arranged with notes, by Francis Turner Palgrave, professor of poetry of the University of Oxford." The copy to hand is a revised and enlarged edition published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co. Professor Palgrave was especially qualified to edit a work of this kind, and no one ' who peruses it can deny that he has done his work admirably. The notes are brief and pertinent, and there a sum- mary of the poetry of the four books- Into ;which the volume is divided. Besides an index of the writers, there is an index of first lines: and nothing, therefore, can be better for ready reference than this" Golden Treasury." Part Ist of volume 3rd is to hand of" Annals of our time ' record of events social and political, home and foreign, from the date of the 15thanniversary of the aCcession of Queen Victoria to the end of the year 1890." This important work is by Mr. H. Hamilton Fyfe, and it is a marvel of research- and condensation. Nothing seems to have been ommitted which is worth noting, and every Item of information is classified in such a way as to be easily accessible. Each page' is headed with the month and year in which the occurrences took place, and in addition to this there is an index which contains an enormous number of references. As a matter of fact there is nothing to equal these " Annals" as a record of comparatively recent events. The "English Illustrated Magazine" is, as usual, a double number for Christmas. The frontispiece is an engraving ()Ca bust of Coleridge's " Christabel." Mr. Alfred Austin sings "The song of the woodpecker," and Sir Samuel Baker has a striking article on "Tigers and tiger-hunting," the illustrations being by Mr. Harry Dixon. Other illustrated articles include" Ancient and modern Eskimos" ; "Fashions of the 19th Century " ; "On gardens and grounds'; "Old city houses " ; and "Women on horseback." There are besides several well illustrated stories, including " A castaway of the south" and "The little mermaid." "Yule Tide " is the name of Cassell's Christmas Annual ; and, like its predecessors, it comes in the first rank, alike for its text and its illustrations. Mr. W. Clarke Russell is the writer of the story of " Mrs. Dine's jewels ; a mid-Atlantic romance." The presentation plate is "The lady with :the lamp," a beautiful representation. of Florence -Nightingale; visiting in the night the hospi- tals at acutari. Two other plates are those of two fair ladies, a blonde and a brunette, by Mr. Arthur Hopkins, and besides these there are in the body, of" Yule-ride " reproductions' Of "The fallen foe," A seasonable sur- prise," and." The carol singers." The " Quiver " Annual, bears the title of "Christmas Arrows," (price 6d.) It contains several special stories of a bright and wholesome kind, all capitally illus- trated.

"The World of Romance," the first part of which is to hand, ale° published by Messrs. Cassell and Co., gives promise of a work which will be alike charming in text and illustrations. With the first part there is a splendid presentation plate of a picture by Mr. Herbert Schmalz, with the title Where is my lord the king?" Messrs. Cassell are likewise issuing, " The history of Don Quixote," by Cervantes, in monthly parts,3d. each, As the illustrations are by that great artist, Gustave Dore, it is not too much to say that no better copy of Don Quixote catebe had. The current issue of" Scribner's Magazine," has for frontispiece " The first Christmas tree," from a fine drawing by Howard Pyle. Amongst the illustrated articles and stories we have "A flood on the Nile," " Espero Gorgoni. Gondolier," "A charge for France," "A painter of beautiful dreams," (Albert Moore) ; "Peter Rugg, the Bostonian," and " The land of Poco Tiernpo." The number is an exceedingly strong one, and nothing can be finer than the reproductions of the beautiful pictures by Albert Moore. 'rho" Graphic " Christmas number is up to its old high level, which is about the best compliment that can be paid toit. The literary fare includes "Ambush against Ambush," by Mr. Archibald Forbes; " The Eulogia," by Mrs. Atherton ; and a third story" Mr. Wright," by Mrs. John Strange Winter. There is quite a number of coloured illustrations, including some of Tom Hood's " Sally Brown." The extra plate picture this year is a reproduction in colours of Ophelia, one of the" Graphic "gallery of Shakespeare's heroines,w hich has been painted by Mr. Marcus Stone, R.A. It is a fine piece of work, though face and figure cannot be said to be so attractive as in some of its predecessors. "Holly Leaves" is the Christmas number of the "Illustrated Sporting and Dramatic News." The coloured picture which is presented with the number is a very charming one, with the title of" Dame Durden," and will deservedly find a permament place in many a home. There are some striking full page plates, includ- ing "At the pantomime," by Fred Marryat ; "Finding the ring," by M. Wilkes; "A maid of Llangollen," and "On Tour." The literary matter is very varied and very readable. The "Pictorial ',World" Christmas number includes two presentation plates, one a large coloured picture from the original by S. E. Walker, entitled "Christmas pensioners," the other a large double page engraving from a drawing by tbe well-known and popular artist, Luis Wain, entitled "Sanctuary." It depicts a pretty Persian cat which is protected from the attacks of a little terrier by a fine dignified bloodhound. There are besides some half-dozen full page plates, and the stories are of a most readable kind. Die " Newbery House Magazine" for December, con- tains, amongst other things, an illustrated article on "Religious education in elementary schools ;" "The service of work ;" "China and its future ;" " Historical sketches ;" "Christmas carols ;" and a Christmas story, with the title "The highwayman." The " Magazine of short stories," (price 6d.) is a double number for Christmas. The stories are excellent, but its great hit is the presentation of a chrorno-litho- graph reproduction of Ricci's celebrated picture "A match for her guardian." It is a wonderful piece of colouring, delicately executed, and, indeed, is worth twice the money which is asked. for magazine and picture. The "Musical Times" for December is accompanied with a Mozart supplement, which is adorned with a number of portraits of the great musician, including one by Hubert Hercomer. There are views of Mozart's birth- place, the house where he lived, and the instruments he used, besides a sketch of his career. The " Strand Magazine " is net lacking in Christmas features ; but does well to continue its portraits of cele- brities. Presented with the December issue is a com- panion picture of the celehrated "Tit-bits." It com- pletes the story which the first picture began, and bears the title of " Scattered Tit-bits."

We have also to hand" The Ladies' Treasury," which is full of good things in relation to literature, educa- tion, and fashion; the Christmas double namber of" The Princess," price 3d., with a presentation plate bearing upon it the title of "Folly ; ' the " Infants' Magazine," "Christmas Chimes," " The family friend," "The family visitor," "The mothers' companion," "Fun Almanack," and "Ally Sloper's Christ mas holi- days."

He examined Hyde's room, and found that every- thing of value had been taken. Then he looked over his own room, and he found it in the same depleted condition. Mr. Jack Hyde had decamped with the watches, jewellery, valuable bric-a-brac, the gambling implements, and every dollar in cash in the place. Mott Reybold swore in a way that alarmed the waiter, for that careful and thrifty gentleman had already got his baggage in such order that he could march at a moment's notice.

Overcome by his feelings, Reybold, as on many other occasions when the tide was setting against him, had recourse to the bottle for courage and comfort. He often boasted of having what convivial men call "a strong head," and this time he tested it to the breaking point, but after hours of almost steady drinking he appeared to be quite as sober as when he began. It must not be imagined that he had lost heart. He still believed, to quote the language of his own profession, that he "had the only winning cards in the pack" in his hands. Curiously enough, his confidence .returned with the darkness. There is something about light that is as withering to crime as frost is to a flower. As he had lost all his money, 'he gambling had been carried on in his place for a week, so that he was not troubled by visitors to-night. He told James that he should not need_him any
more till the morrow, =a that he was tree to gio, to his home, if he had one, a privilege of whiah• the prudent James • speddily availed himself.

Soon after ten o'clock Reybold • changed his fashionable dress for rougher clothes, and in other ways disguised himself, so that his most Intimate friend—not even Jack Hyde—would have recognised him at night if he met him on the street.
Feeling more secure than he had since, he read that notice in the paper in the morning; he locked the door of his apartments and descende4 to the. street.
It was raining, and he was glad of this, for it drove all those. who had homes worth, going to from the street.

He knew full well whithes he was bound to- night, but he had no definite mission in view, ex- cept to learn more about that " confession," if it were possible, and to find out from Cash if Frank Lefferts, in his ravings, had said anything about a forgery. After much twisting and looking behind, as it he were trying to baffle a pursuit, he can to the squat house occupied by Cash and his wife. He knocked, and no reply coming, he knocked a second and a third time with increasing energy. At length a window opened above his head, and Cash called down: "Who's there ? "
Mott,Reybold," dame the reply. "The devil ! "

And Reybold did hurry up, but an officer, watching on the next corner, saw him enter the house.

div.head: MESSROOM INCIDENT.
div.p: A MESSROOM INCIDENT.

It was in India. Dinner was just finished in the •Messrobm;and sevetal English officers were pitting about the table. Their bronzed: faces had the Set but not unkindly look common among military men.. The conversation at, best had not been anim- ated, and just now there was a lull, as the night was too hot for small talk. The,major of the regi went, a clean-cut man of 55, turned towards his neighbour at the table, a young subaltern, who Wag leaning back in his chair with his hands clasped be- hind his head, staring through cigar smoke at the ceiling. The major was slowly looking the man over, from his handsome face down, when,with a sudden alertness, and in a quiet, steady voice, he said :--" Don't move, please, Carruthers. I want to try an experiment with you. Don't move a muscle." "All right, major," replied the subaltern, without 'even turning his eyes.: "Hadn't the least idea a moving, I assure you. What's the game ? " By this time all the others were listening in a lazily ex- pectant way. "Do you think, continued the major, and his voice trembled just a little, "Do you think you could keep absolutely, still for, say,two minutes to save your lite ? " "Are you, joking ? " " On. the contrary move a muscle and you are o dead. man. Can you bear the strain." The subaltern, barely whispered" Yes,"and his face paled slightly. "Burke," said the Major addressing an officer across the table," pour some of that milk into a saucer, and set it on the floor here just behind me. Gently man! Quiet ! " Not a word was spoken as the officer quietly filled the saucer, walked With it carefully round the table, and set it down whet* the major had indicated on the floor. Like a marble statue sat the young subaltern, in his white linen clothes, while a cobra di capello, which had beeh crawling up the legs of his trousers, slowly raised its head, then turned, descended to the floor, and glided towards the milk. 'Suddenly the silence was broken by the report of the major's revolver, and the snake lay dead on the floor. "Thank you, major," said the subaltern, us the two men shook hands warmly. ." You have saved my life." "You're welcome, my boy," replied the senior." "But -011 did your share."
PRIMITIVE METHODISM AT WARRING- . TON. SUNDAY SCHOOL WORK.

A conference of Sunday school workers, of the Warrington and Widnes Primitive Methodist cir- cuit,.was held in the Chapel, Legh-street, Warring- ton on Monday afternoon. The subject of the conference was the present aspect of Sunday school work in the circuit.

In the evening a public meeting was held, Mr. J. Dodda presiding. The Rev. Dr. FERGUSON in an address, referred at length to his experience in America, and afterwards touched on one of the great social questions of the day, viz., the homeless. lie said that there were 300,000 homeless families in London, which meant that about 900,000 persons were without a home of thefs own to go to. It was a great difficulty, and he thought that the State should take some steps towards providing for these people. He suggested that some of the millions which were spent annually upon maintaining the army and navy should be expended in this direction, or some of the hundreds of 'thousands of pounds which were wasted annually on liquor could be applied more profit- ably in resuscitating the people he had referred to. The speaker then touched on some of the attendant evils ,of football. He wished it to be understood that legitimate sport was necessary, but he would like to say something about the demoralizing influence of the game, which was obtaining a great hold on the English public. rhe per- sons who indulged in this "running after a piece of leather" were becoming subject to heart disease. The doctor proclaimed that the excite- ment attendant on the game cau:ed too great a pressure 'on the heart, and gave rise to the evil which he had before mentioned. What was recreation to one man was destruction to another. It was neces- sary perhaps for a young man who had been confined to a desk all day to go into the fields and run and jump,but in the case of men employed at forges and collieries the proper place for them after their day's work was over was to go home, and alter a rest to put their feet in slippers and then read,for mental improvement. Now-a- days this class of men usually played taxing games, and, tried their constitutions too much, and would ultimately have to reap the harvest of the seed which they were now sowing. The rev, gentleman animadverted strongly' on the number of clubs. These places, he submitted, were merely facilities for procuring drink, and were,con- eequently as great 'a danger as public-houses. They pr.- vented men also from going home to help their wives in the education of their children. The speaker then concluded by hoping the classes would be opened where both sexes could meet for social purposes, and where' bath would have opportunities for mental improvement.' The Rev. C. F. FisTen having addressed the meeting, - The Rev. W. TnonNLxv read a report on the present aspect of Sunday school work in the Warrington and Widnes circuit. The reverend gentleman observed that they had five schools in the circuit. In March last there were 89 teachers, 79, of these were members of the church. The average attendance of teacher was, morn- ing, 32 ; afternoon, 54. According to the latest reports, there were 93 teachers, an increase of 4 ; 81 of whom were members of the church, an increase of 2. The aver- age attendance was : morning 28, afternoon 54. So that in regard teachers, observed the speaker, they were in a, better position. In March, there were 785 scholars forty of whom only were members of the church; 14 were under 14 years of age, and 26 above 14 years of age. The average attendance of scholars was: Morn- ing, .234; afternoon, 406. There were at the present date 825 scholars, an increase of 40. He could not say how many of these children were members of the church, as the secretaries of the schools had not sup, plied the information in the reports. He presumed ,how- ever, that there was an increased number of children- who were members of the church, for they had done gocd work in Widnes and Simms' Cross Schools. A new society class had been formed at Widnes for the young. people. He had recently written tickets for eighteen candidates. The average attendance of scholars was : Morning 274, an increase of 40; afternoon 452, increase 46. It would, therefore, be seen that they had only to. mourn the dscreasein the average Of teachers on Sunday mornings, viz., three. He was confident that the figures which he had read were correct. In some stations the t Circuit Sunday School Union meant very little,a.s nearly all the work pertaining to it was done by the preacher. In this circuit the Committee did itS Work. The Secre- tary kept a sharp eye on the schools, he was glad o say. In his reference to the work which was going on in Widnes and Simms' Cross, he omitted to say that during , the past quarter a good number of children had joined Sunday school work the church. The present aspect on . in the circuit was of a pleasing and encouraging charac- ter, as he had reports stating that progress was being made in all, or nearly all, departments. (Applause.) The meeting ended with the usual votes of thanks.

div.head: LIE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: LIE SHIP CANAL.
A SHAREHOLDERS' PROTECTION. LEAGUE

Steps are being taken to form aa association of Ship Cathil shareholders for protective purposes. It is pointed out that the oldest debenture holders and the Corpora- tion, with their loan of £3,000,000, are practically safe. The unfortunate shareholders, by paying for everybody's blunders and extravagences, have seen the value of their property shrink from £8,000,000 to £3,500,000, .
-ALLEGED EXTRAVAGANCE AND MISMANAGE- MENT.

The Manchester City Council met on Wednesday to consider the affairs of the Ship Canal Company. A letter was read from Lord Egerton of Tatton, chairman of the Company, explaining some matters in connection with the alleged extravagance of the administration of only arose when the Company were obliged in Novem- ber, 1890, either to take over the contract or stop the works. The salaries given by the contractor and after- wards by the Compauy to a few responsible officials were large, but the engagements were only for a limited period,, and no bonuses were promised except on the con- dition that the work should be done to the satisfaction of the Board. The Company were prepared to have all matters of administration fully investigated. In a further letter from the various Directors of the Company it was stated that if the Council should be of opinion that the interests of all concerned would be furthered by a greatet control of the spending departments being given to the Corporation's representatives on the Board they would loyally and cordially fall in with such an arrangement. The letters having been read, the Council proceeded to consider the report of the Consultative Ship Canal Committee. The discussion turned on an amendment moved by Mr. Bunson in- structing the Committee to take immediate steps to increase the number of Corporation directors, on the Ship Canal Board to eight, being a majority of the Board. Alderman Sir John Harwood, Mr. J. W. Southern, Mr. Alderman Thompson, Mr. R. Gilson, and a large number of members took part in the debate. The amendment was rejected by a small majority, and the report was approved. COMMERCIAL BEARING OF THE CANAL.

Whilst so mnch is being said about the extra cost of completing the Ship Canal, it is as well to have in mind that the commercial aspect of the case still continues good We take the following from a recent lecture upon the subject by Mr. Marshall Stevens :—The dock accom- modation of Manchester and Salford alone was greater than than that of Bristol or Cardiff. And for three miles further down outside the docks the Canal was widened an additional 50 feet so as to provide for vessels to lie along the whole ef one side without further widening. Practically, the Canal was a huge dock from Manchester to the sea. As to railway communication at the Man- chester and Salford Docks, they had the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway which was about to spend £400.000 or £500,000 to get communication with the Canal; they had also the London and North-Western and the Great Western, the Midland, Great Northern, and Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire. Recently the manager of the last-named company was examined, and he said the company expected to get three million tons of traffic in connection with the Canal. Hardly a town of any im- portance in the district but would be brought directly into communication with the Manchester Ship Canal. With reference to the accommodation at the docks, the Canal authorities had allocated certain of the berths for regular lines of traders. The highest docks at Manches- ter would be almost entirely appropriated by regular lines of coasting steamers, and there was not a single line of coasting steamers running from Liverpool at present whose owners had not made application for regular berths. The Manchester Canal was nearer to the South Yorkshire coalfield than any of the trade ports on the east coast. The output of coal in the district nearest the canal than any other port was greater than the total aggregate out- put of Northumberland, Durham and South Wales corn- bened.TheY would fini it was so from the Board of Trade returns. He was not speaking of the coal exported, but simply of the output. The canal would be nearer than any other ocean steamer port to 'a population of 7i millions of people, one-fifth of the population of the whole of the United Kingdom. The area the canal would serve in this way was 7,500 sq. miles, about 1-16th of the area of the United Kingdom. In the district the canal would serve there were some 200 industrial towns, there was hardly a port in the United Kingdom which did not tci 'a very considerable extent, exchange traffic with Manchester and District. And by means of a canal they should open a new coast trade, which, whilst it would benefit Manchester, would also benefit the country at large. ' The maximum charge for the Ship Canal was , made up of one half the charges payable to Mersey Dock and Harbour Authorities and one half the railway rate to and from Manchester. They might take it that the merchant saved half and that the canal got the other half. The Canal charged on goods, and they would get on an average about the same toll out of the goods a ship was carrying as the toll a ship paid in passing through the Suez Canal. The maximum charges on ship oould not exceed the existing charges on ship at Liverpool. A railway company might carry goods for nothing and still be unable to compete with the Canal. True, the extra distance was 35 miles, and the extra cost to the owner in travelling that distance would be about three decimal something. The canal did not count upon revenue from ships as ships, but upon the goods they carried.

Wilier route to the gantry we have just described: The Old Quay Docks walls are gradually beihg destroyed,and the stones removed, the least valuable of them to form the outer pitching of the Canal wall here, the others to be re-drassed as new for other masonry work in connec- tion with the Ship Canal. The old connection between the Runcorn and Latchford Canal and the Old Quay Decks was originally ,spanned by a movable bridge, which gave access to various works; this, when the old canal was abolished, gave place to a timber erection high enough to allow the Ship Canal traffic to be car- ried underneath. This timber erection will, in,a few Months, give place to a permanent swina-bridge, worked like the others along the Ship Canal by hydraulic power. This, which is known as the Old Quay Swing- bridge, is now in course of erection, by Messrs. Arrol, of Glasgow, and, closely adjoining, the hydraulic tower is rapidly rising and becoming a feature in the landscape.

div.head: TIMBER POND,
div.p: A TIMBER POND,

Just outside the Western Marsh lock at the Weaver there is a large timber pond, formed by the Weaver embankment, which, forms the north bank of the Ship Canal, which by penning up thg water of that river as far as Frodsham, will form efloat for timber storage i and a dock available for the larger vessels three miles n length. STEAM FERRIES.

It is contemplated to construct steam ferries at Hulme's Bridge and Main Boat on the Canal. Plans for these have been submitted by Mr. Leader Williams to the High- way Board of that district, and negotiations are passing on the matter. Shortly there will be a series at the Manchester end.

div.head: DONT FORGET ADAMSON
div.p: DONT FORGET ADAMSON

The new Mayor of Manchester, Mr. Bosdin T. Leech, recently alluded to the originator and pioneer of the canal, Mr. Daniel Adamson. There exists no more fitt- ing man than Mr. Leech, to carry out the suggestion he gave, when he uttered the words" tribute to the memory of Daniel Adamson and his great work, which Manchester would, one day, pay him." Why should not the Mayor of Manchester initate a project for this object, something of a worthy and useful nature, which might be in readiness for opening simultaneously with the canal itself.

div.head: RIVER WEAVER, &c.
div.p: RIVER WEAVER, &c.

From Ellesmere Port to the River Weaver, there is little of moment going on. Here and there ,gangs of men are working at some slipped portion of the bank, but altogether a walk along the bank of this length is about as tame as the passage up or down in a boat is pleasant. The bank eastwards from the famous Weaver sluices is being pushed forward, and as the bank acquires sufficient breadth the pitching on the estuary side of it is most vißorously 'proceeded with. Here the dressed stones are of exceptional size and weight, being from about fire tons upwards. The work of bank-making in a river is necessarily very slow. The gantry appears to have been most rapidly and successfully completed. The tipping was commenced from this completed gantry, and it is pro- posed to continue it almost witholit intermission until that spotin the riVer is reached where it is intended to construct the new Weston 111eisey lock. This lock, when complete& will provide accommodation for vessels which it is desired to pass from the River Mersey across the Ship Canal to the Weaver Navigation. -

MOORE AND ACTON GRANGE.

From. this swing bridge to the completed Bridge at Moore Lane, is a very 'busy length, but chiefly with the necessary .excavation required for so deep a cutting. At Acton Grange, the whole of the five girders for the high level railway bridge are in course of construction, and a most stupendous piece of work it is, very interest- ing, whether viewed from below or inspected at closer quaiters on the platform. Visitors who desire to climb to the higher level, to either inspect the bridge, or obtain a view of the surrounding scenery, may do so here with moderate comfort, for a set of 90 steps has been placed up the bank for ~the convenience of th 9 workmen.

div.head: LATCHFORD SECTION.
div.p: LATCHFORD SECTION.

Round about Latchford the operations are numerous. At Wilderspool the concreting of the bridge pier is in progress as well 'as the rest' for the end of the swing bridge ;at this spot the old bridge remains intact, there has been no temporary erection, therefore the new bridge will have to somewhat divert this road, the new road passing along the back of some houses, the other sides of which front the present road. The tipping on the south side of the canal for the Latchford high-level road bridge has gone on so well that workmen are engaged in levelling the slope of the bank, and the abutment to receive this bank is now being built. On the north side of the Canal the work is a little bewildering, as the new road will have to get to the high level of the new station without interfering with the traffic going on below, and so piers are springing up here and there', destined, in a 'short time to support the arches necessary for this road. besides the work already named there is near here the erection of the new railway station and the construction of the very long platforms ; also the construction of the Knutsford-road swing bridge and the high level railway bridge. These, together with the construction of the locks, and the building of the hydraulic house near the hospital, form an amount of work going on unequalled in any other portion of the same length. .

div.head: BARTON, Sze.
div.p: BARTON, Sze.

At Barton the work. at the aqueduct is progressing. and the swing road bridge will soon be in course of erection, the roller path being safely down. The tim- bering for the erection of this road bridge is being formed from the pieces taken down frotn'the aqueduct where they were done with. The gates to Mode Wheel Locks are nearly completed, and the hydraulic work for opening and closing these gates is rapidly being got into position. Some cracks have been noticed in the concrete wall of the Stretford Dock, caused by the shift- ing character of the ground, and piling is being resorted to to secure the safety of this portion of the work. A SWING BRIDGE OF 2,000 TONS.

The most important feature is the commencement of the swing-bridge, which will connect the two banks of the Canal, and form a portion of Trafford-road. The roller path is safely down, the hydraulic ram fixed in the centre,and the erection of the bridge has actually begun. The total weight of this bridge will be over 2,000 tons, each of the 64 steel rollers to assist in the turning weigh- ing 35cyrt, or more; and all the steel work, which is rapidly being delivered on to the ground, appears to be of the same substantial character. This bridge, which is said to be the largest swing-bridge in the United King- dom, is being constructed by Messrs. Butler and Co., of Leeds, and its construgtion will be watched with interest by large nutlibers of visitors. It will form one of a rather remarkable series of bridges to form Trafford-road. In the first place is the girder bridge over the Cheshire Lines ; next, closely adjoining,is the girder bridge over the Bridgewater Canal (these latter girders have ;only been placed in position this last month) ; next comes a girder bridge over the traffic line of the Ship Canal Company, then comes the swing bridge hereip described, and then, at a very, short distance,comes the Old Trafford bridge across the river. It was expected by many peo- ple that this bridge would be taken down; but that will not be the case, the river will still flow under it and form a lay-by for some of the smaller boats. '
THE WEAVER WATERWAY AND RUNCORN DOCKS.
An article on "The benefits conferred by the Man- chester Ship Canal on other canal systems and enter- prises," in the "Ship Canal News," says:—

- A little further up the canal we come to the Weaver, worked by the Weaver Navigation Trustees, a committee 13 of Cheshire gentlemen, who are appointed 37 the county, and act in an honorary capacity. Entrance to this water is obtained from the canal by means of the Weston Marsh Lock. The Weaver runs through Northwich to Winsford, near Middlewich, thus passing through the heart of the Cheshire salt district. The rise of the Wea- ver, at the inland end is 37ift., above the height at the Ship Canal end. At Anderton is fixed a lift which trans- fers vessels to or from the Weaver and the Trent and Mer- Toy Canal ; the difference in the level of these two canals is 50ft. lin. The Weaver can accommodate vessels of 350 tons cargo, with a 10ft. draught • but when some small dredging improvements have been made it is expected that vessels of 800 to 1,000 tons will be enabled to use this waterway. - - -

The Weaver is about the only waterway that has im- proved with modern engineering.• Half a century ago it possessed 12 locks, and could only accommodate vessels of 60 toes. Now it is hoped, as just stated, to manage a 1,000 tons vessel in this waterway. That such posses- sions as the Weaver are worthy the fostering care of this county in which they are situated, the account of the concern prove. In the year ending March, 1889, the trustee paid over te the county £16,148, the profit of the trust,this mAney being applied to the relief of the county rates: The opening of the Canal is almost certain to greatly increase the influence of the Weaver. Again,one of the most favoured of the Birmingham Ship Canal schemes takes the Weaver and Manchester. Ship Canal as a portion of its route. The exports of all amount to 1,000,000 tons yearly. The other chief exports using the Weaver are stone, burnt ore, soda, and other chemicals. The imports consist of pottery materials, such as china clay, china stone, flints, and bone ash, also hides. The Weaver Trustee have an agreement with the Canal Company that vessels carrying salt only, and exceeding 450 tons grpss register, and carrying not more than 500 tons, shall pass from the Weaver and out of the Canal at Eastham, or up the Canal to Runcorn Docks, free of all dues or tolls, also that vessels light or in ballast, destined for the Weaver for a salt cargo, shall use the Ship Canal free. Other vessels with cargoes of flint, felspar, china, stone, china clay, or bones for use in the manufacture of, pottery, not exceeding 450 tons gross register, or more than 500 tons cargo, may use the Canal up to Weston Point by payment of half the ordinary ship dues, and should the cargo be,bound for the Staffordshire Potteries it will be permitted to pass up the Canal to the Weaver it one-half the ordinary Ship Canal tolls. Passing further up the Canal, we come to Runcorn, a seaport, with Customs regulations, and accompanying privilege of bending goods. The quays, etc., are well equipped and adapted for general traffic. There are seven wet docks, the whole of which—basins, docks, and warehouses—are the property of the Ship Canal Com- pany, who are also the proprietors of it fleet of powerful tugs, which tow sea-going vessels free of charge. The port of Runcorn, or rather the portion of it which makes the town a port, being the property of the Ship Canal Company, there is no stated reduction of dues or tolls for vessels during the Canal for delivery at Runcorn. But great advantages are conferred in other ways. For instance, at the present time only vessels of light draught can be taken up with safety, the water being only 16i feet at spring tides and about 10 feet at neap. Once the Canal is opened, vessels of any size will be able to go up at any state of the tide. The yearly traffic passing through the Runcorn docks is on an average 60,000 craft ; the average imperts is some 50,000 tons, the number of vessels using the port being about 4,000. The imports consist of china clay, blue clay, pig iron, slates, road stones, and miscellan- eous articles. The exports consist of salt and coals. There is also a large barge traffic with other Mersey ports. Runcorn is the Mersey terminal of the Bridgewater Canal System, the property of the Ship Canal Company. The traffic of this undertaking in 1888 was 2,916,754 tons, 914,867 tons of this being carried by the Company, as carriers, and the remainder by other carriers.

div.head: MURDER OF A BOY.
div.p: THE MURDER OF A BOY.

Samuel Crawford, aged nine years, and Robert Shear on, aged eight years, were on Wednesday at the Liver- pool assizes found guilty of the murder of a boy named David Dawson Eccles, at Liverpool on September 7,last. The jury held that the prisoners in consequence of their tender age were not responsible for their actions.
PRINCE PLESS AND MISS .CORNWALLIS
WEST.

The marriage of Prince Pless and Miss Cornwallis West was solemnized at St. Margaret's,Westminster, on Tues- day, in the presence of a fashionable congregation, in- cluding Prince Edward of Saxe-Weimar and several foreign ministers. The bride, who wore pearl satin, was given away by her father.

div.head: EXAMINER', SATURDAY, DECEIVW4 12, 1891. THE LIBERAL BAZAAR.
div.p: THE EXAMINER', SATURDAY, DECEIVW4 12, 1891. THE LIBERAL BAZAAR.
CONVERSAZIONE AND PRESENTATION AT
THE CO-OPERATIVE HALL.

As a commemoration of the recent very success- ful Liberal Bazaar, in Warrington, a conversazione was, on Monday evening, held in the Co-operative Sankey-st. The conversazione had been got up by a number of leading Liberals in the town, and invitations to it were sent to all the workers in connection with the bazaar, and to members of the troupe of Warrington Amateur Christy Mins- trels, and others who assisted in one way or another at the bazaar. There was a large response to these invitations. All the arrangements for the gather- ing had been efficiently carried out under the direc- tions of a committee of which Mr. T. Birchall was the chairman. The walls and windows of the large hall had been hung with curtains and mirrors, and presented an elegant and cheerful appearance. The entrance passage and stairs were laid with carpets, and several smaller apartments were arranged as cloakrooms, &c. During the evening refreshments, which had been supplied by Mr. Chantry, of Horse- market-st., were handed round. There were also on view,under the charge of Councillor F. W. Monks and Mr. W. H. Woodcock, several microscopes, and by means of these there was a very interesting dis- play of objects, selected with a view to meeting the tastes of a mixed audience. The guests as they arrived were received by Mr. T. Birchall, on behalf of the Committee, and amongst those present were Mrs. Z. Armitage, Mr. and Mrs. W. Pierpoint, Coun- cillor and Mrs. J. 11. Fleming, Councillor and Mrs. H. Roberts, Councillor and Mrs. A. Browne' Council- lor and Mrs. Shaw-Green, Councillor and Mrs. Bea- man, Dr. Gornall, Mr. F. R. Roberts, Mr. J. C. Holmes, Mr. J. Walker, Mr. Blackhurst, jun., Mr. G. Clay, Mr. P. Silcock, Mr. Corney,Mr. John Gandy, Mr. J. Mounfield, jun., Mr. A. H. Rathbone, Mr. I. Hayward, Mr. J. Hayward, Mr. S. Jones, Mr. S. Kenyon, Mr. A. Lee, Mr. E. J. Mitchell, Mr. A. Pickatance, &c. _ . _

The earlier part of the evening was taken up with the rendering of a short musical programme. The programme was opened with a selection, " Norma,' by Mr. T. R. Ford's band. Mr. H. Yonge then sang,in excellent style, "The Goodwin Sands," and he was followed by a pleasing solo on the auto-harp by Mr. Bennett. Miss Locker gave an expressive ren- dering of "The better land," and Miss Coubrough's singing of" Robin Adair;' was much admired. A capital clarionet solo by Sergeant Riches brought the programme to a close. An interesting part of the proceedings, was the presentation to Mr. C. Jackson Holmes ot a set of silver fish knives and forks and a silver cake basket, as.a recognition of his great services as general secretary of the bazaar committee. The cake basket is of soliel silver, of antique pattern and richly chased. The fish knives and forks have handsome ivory handles and engraved blades. They bear the following inscription, "Presented to C. Jackson Holmes by the workers of the Liberal Bazaar in re- cognition of his kindly services as secretary, War- rington, October, 1891." The articles were supplied by Messrs. G. Blackhurst and Son, Saukey-st. Mr. T.Binds.s.LL,who presided at the presentation, said he was extremely sorry to find himself in that position that night, but their chairman, Mr. F. A. Roberts, living so far away or for some reason or other, was not able to be with them, so they had to be content With himself as a substitute. In the first place, allow him to offer them on behalf of the bazaar Committee, a most hearty welcome. They offered their sincere congratulations to the ladies for the very great success which attended their efforts at the late bazaar. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the absence of Mr. John Rylands, he said it would have been a satisfaction to them to have had a repre- sentive of the family of Rylands present, a family which had been so intimately associated with 'Liberalism in Warrington, and which had done so much for the cause they all had at heart. (Hear, hear.) There was another friend too whose absence they very much deplored, and that was •their good friend Miss Bessie Dutton. (Applause.) Hiss Dutton wrote saying how greatly she regretted not being able to accept the invitation, as she had a long-standing engagement to fill in Harrogate on that evening. With much disappointment she had to forego the pleasure of being with them, and she also much deplored missing the pleasure and satiss faction of witnessing the presentation to Mr. Holmes, who had been such a kindly and untiring helper to them all. (Applause.) Mr. Birchall then called upon Mrs. Z. Armitage to make the presenta- tion. _ _ _

Mrs. Z. ARMITIGB, who was received with applause. said it was a pleasure to her to have to ask Mr.Holmes's acceptance of that present from the workers Of the Liberal bazaar. Mr. Holmes had been an untiring secretary, and had done a large amount of work with great kindness and great tact. (Hear, hear and applause.). He had—should she say ?—kept peace amongst them. (Ap?lause and laughter.) Mrs. Armitage then, Amidst applause, asked Mr. Holmes's acceptance pf the present. Mr. W. PIERPOINT, in response to calls from the audience,very heartily thanked Mr. Holmes for the very earnest efforts lie had made on behalf of the Liberal bazaar. It had been his (Mr. Pierpoint's) first experience of a bazaar and it had been .an exceed- ingly pleasant one—in fact he did not care how soon they had another bazaar. (Applause and laughter.) They had done very well in the last one, and he felt sure that, if ever the occasion arose, that they should require another bazaar, the ladies would work just as hard, or perhaps harder, and the result would be even more successful than with the bazaar in which they had just participated. (Applause.) Councillor H. ROBERTS also spoke in compliment- ary terms of Mr. Holmes. He did not know whether Mr. Holmes had any temper or not, but from the firAt to the last there had been no evid- ence of it. He did not think itwould have pos- sible to find another man in the ranks of their party who could have worked from the inception of the bazaar to the end so entirely free from all unplea- santness. It was generally considered that, a bazaar should end in a row, but their bazaar had been an exception to that rule, and in a large de- gree that was due to the tact of Mr. Holmes. ( Hear, hear.) He hoped that before long they should

have Mr. Holmes in a more useful capacity as a public man in Warrington. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN said that during the bazaar he was continually in contact with the Secretary in arranging for different matters, and, he must say that the perfect ease and comfort with which every- thing was Carried on astonished him, and he quite 6ndoreed what Mr. Roberts had said; that there was no other man in the party, mad especially a young man, who could have done the work with the same ease and ability as Mr. Holmes had done it. (Hear, hear and applause.) Mr. C. J. HOLM" who was cordially received, said he was sure they would readily believe "him when he said that he felt it exceedingly difficult at that moment to find words to anything like ade- quately thank them for that most handsome present The ladies who had the choosing of the'present had shown most excellent taste in the beautiful articles which they had bought, and he trusted he might long be the possessor of them to, remind him of the pleasant days they spent together working, for the good of that cause which they all had so much at heart. (Hear, hear.) The bazaar was undoubtedly a great success, but he really Couldnot take all the credit which they had been good enough to give him. He often thought as the work was proceed- ing that those people who were engaged in a much less conspicuous manner certainly deserved more credit than they got,and to share in any honour that might have been given at.the finish. Apart, alto- gether, from the financial question the bazaar was a triumph, because it brought them all into close contact 'with each other and showed their leaders that, when occasion required, they, could depend upon the rank and file, and upon every individual member of the party, as in the days of 1880. (Hear hear.) Mr. Birchall had alluded to the work done by the ladies, and it appeared to him that the chief credit of the success as regarded the bazaar, was most decidedly to be given to Mrs. Armitage and those ladies who so gallantly supported her in their labourious work. (Hear hear, and applause.) Without their valuable help they really could not have had any bazaar at all, and now that they had got the ladies so publicly and emphatically secured on their side, there was no doubt whatever as to the position of the Liberal party in the future. (Applause.) Speaking more particularly with regard to those ladies and gentlemen who had been good enough to subscribe to that testimonial,he was exceedingly obliged to them for it, and he trusted that they might long be spared to work together for the good of the Liberal party, that their work might be brought to a successful issue, and' that they might by that means be enabled to return a man to Parliament who would represent their shade of opinion, and would be governed by that true principle of Liberalism—" by the people and for the people," and by that means they should be able to raise this borough once more from the al- most forgotten days of Toryism to the higher realms of Liberalism. (Applause.) Mr. T. MORRIS then • moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman for the strenuous and arduous work he had done in promoting the success of the bazaar.

Councillor FLiMING seconded this proposal, which was carried by acclamation, and the CHAIR- MAN suitably responded. Dancing was afterwards indulged in to the strains of Mr. Ford's band, Mr. T. Morris acting as M.C. An exceedingly pleasant evening was spent.

"3s. 11D. MAN'S ESTIMATE OF MAN."
The usual weekly meeting of the Penketh WesleYan Mutual Improvement Society was held on Wednesday evening, Mr. Snoddy in the chair. There was a good attendance.

Mr. Peers read a short paper entitled "3s. 11d.ee. man's estimate of man," in which he said the very prevalent practice of marking goods at a penny less than the next whole shilling, as 2s. 11d. for 35., 3s. 11d. for 45., indicates a wide, firmly established consensus of shopkeeping opinion as to the want of noes- and general gullibility of mankind at large. The great principle of 3s. 11d. may , be traced in social life, *here Smith, Brown,Jones, and Robinson are trying to impose upon each other, at each other's expense. In law, where the adepts get the oyster and the clients the shells. The same on the turf; while the advertising columns of our newspapers show, that even the greatest absurdity, if only repeated often enough, receives unhesitating accept- ance. But it is in those two great spherea of opinion, Politics and Religion, that this great principle is most manifested. When men, leaving the concrete trivalities of their every-day life, come to , deal with the more abstract ideas of Religion and Politics and to use, on unaccustomed subjects, their tun Exercised reasoning faculties, we then see most of their " mostly " side. Perhapatbe most conspicuous,eviclence of this ls "the Conservative working-man." The conservatism of the class from which our hereditary legislators are drawn, and of others somewhat similarly situated,is quite under- standable. They wished to.keep political power in their ; own hands, and were naturally averse to changes.. But how the class so long misrepresented and whose claim to a voice in the choosing of representatives was so long, ' so scornfully, 'and contemptuously rejected, can have such short memories and so little self-respect as to sup- port their erewhile scorners, is only to be understood upon the Carlylean hypothesis. And the climax of poli- tical self-stultification is reached when he, the lately Tory-kicked one, succumbs to the blandishments of the Primrose Dames and falls a prey to such a shallow device fer political inveiglement. In -considering the relation of the" mostly" in conjunction with the political axiom that" majorities must rule," we are brought face to face with the question :—lf Carlyle's dictum is an axiom is not the rule of the majority necessarily the rule of folly? Undoubtedly an aristocratic government would be the best—if you could get it and keep it. But unfortun- ately the aristos, like other of this world's goods, is liable to deteriorate by keeping. Leaving the platform for the pulpit, we find folly still in the majority. Nay, does not the very existence of the pulpit itself afford conclusive evidence that in religious, as in other circles, the " mostly "do mostly predominate? Just fancy the transparent absurdity of allowing a man the privilege of shutting himself up in a box and rating you, without fear of contradiction, for a whole half-hour. And that, too,for sins you never committed and for which you are not responsible. In seine cases the box is not big enough, but may contain a hogshead. Here again we have to ask ourselves what estimate can the preachers and teachers of religion have formed of the reasoning power of their congregations? Before answering this, we have to ask another question :—How are we to estimate the preachers themselves? Upon the answer to this de- pends the answer to the first. l‘low,very little reflection will convince us that the clergy are not picked men. They are rather a sample than a selection from the people. They are not selected for their originality, or as having any peculiar power of thought. Hence they mete out to others their own measure. When, "A rowsin' whid at times they vend, and nailt wi' Scrip- ture" they expect their audience to believe it because they do so themselves. But how, if our estimate of the clergy had been different, had been more favourable to theirintellectual superiority; if we had found them possessed of that heaven-born superiority which should distinguish men who profess to guide others over the trackless regions transcending experience? Viewed then in the . light that the clergy ought to be, as teachers of eternal truth, men of exceptional in- tellectual and moral insight, we can only in- fer that if their office does confer this faculty upon them, it is most shockingly abused. In this case Viley are not only" blind leaders of the blind " coillusionists with their flock—but wilful and deliberate misleaders of the people—advancing statements which, on the above assumption, they must know to be untrue. Pulpit oratory affords. abundant examples of this ; 'out one well marked instance shall suffice. This is the per- sistent advancement of the" aboriginal idea," of the origin of our race—man's first state being one of per- fection. All " knowledge " all logical inference from facts runs counter to this. The earliest evidence of man upon earth showed him to have lived in a state of semi- human savagery—the user ef the rudest forms of flint implements. But who ever heard this truth announced from the pulpit? Never • but in its place the old unten- able hypothesis—from which are deduced conclusions equally untenable ! The conclusion I arrive at is that untruths should not be reiterated—even from a pulpit ! In charity we must assume the reiterators not to see them as untruths. Herein time will be their teacher. But the lesson will first be learned by the laity, who will shame their teachers into accepting it. The paper was commented upon by Messrs. D. Gar- nett, C. E. Parker, the Chairman, A. White, and H. S. Jones. The essayist was replying when the Chairman closed the meeting abruptly by announcing the Doxo- logy.
