HAYDOCK COLLIERS IN Couirr.—Ralph Talbot, a collier, at Haydock, sued Thomas Reed, a checkweighman, living at Church-road, Haydock, for £l5 13s. 6d. b;..lance of money lent, and interest. Mr. H. J. Longton, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. A. Browne, defended. It appeared from the opening statement of Mr. Longtori that the transaction in dispute originated in the year 1879. Defendant at that time, saying he was in trouble came to plaintiff and asked him to lend him some money- to prevent him from being sold up. Plaintiff said his money was invested in the Earlestown Building Sxietyf and-that he was receiving 5 per cent. for it. Defendant said he would give him the same interest, and plaintiff thereupon agreed to lend defendant £44: Since the money was lent, defendant had paid plain- tiff Various sums at different times, but he had declined to pay the balance which was now sued for, hence the present action. Ralph Talbot, the plaintiff, on being put in the box corroborated the state- ments of his solicitors. Cross-examined by Mr. Browne, he said he could neither read or write, but on being pur- sured he admitted that he could write his name, and he wrote his:name on a piece of paper handed to him by Mr. Browne. A receipt for £ll 10s. was handed to him but he swore that he had never signed his name which ap- peared upon it, and had never received the £ll 10s. rhis denial he adhered to, after being told by the judge to carefully look at the document and not to answer rashly. Nancy Talbot, the wife of the plaintiff, and Winifred Halsall, a former housekeeper, also gave evi- dence. Mrs. Halsall admitted that the defendant had paid her two or three sums which she gave to plaintiff, but which the latter did not appear to have given defendant credit for.—For the defence, Reed stated that he paid the £ll 103. to plaintiff at his (Reed's) own house, and he drew up the receipt produced at plaintiff's own re- quest, and to this plaintiff wrote his name. He also spoke to having paid three separate sums of £l. 10s., £2, and £1 10s. to Mrs. Halsall to be given to the plaintiff. —ln giving judgment, his Honour said he came to the conclusion that plaintiff had signed the receipt for the £ll 103., and he also gave defendant credit for the money he had paid through Mrs. Halsall. He gave a veedict for plaintiff for 14s. 6d. only, which sum he cal- culated to be due as interest.

A DISCARDED HORSE.—Mary Jane Maler, of Gregson- st., Deansgate, Manchester, beer-house keeper and horse owner, sued Thomas Shepherd, of Lymm, fishmonger, for £B, the claim being for return of money paid by plaintiff to defendant on the 3rd September in connec- tion with the purchase of a horse. Mr. Ryla,nce, of Manchester, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. A. Browne, defended. It appeared that the defendant had sold the plaintiff a horse for £B, and it was alleged en behalf of the plaintiff, that when the bargain was made the defendant said that if the horse did not suit he would pay plaintiff her money back again. Plaintiff in her evi- dence corroborated this statement, but another witness named Frank Bailey, who had been with her when the purchase was effected, cOntradicted her in several res- pects. Other witnesses were called to prove that the horse after being tried was sent back to Lymm, and left in Pepper-st., but that it eventually got into a field be- longing to Mr. John Legh, wheelwright, where it had remained ever since.—Mr. Browne for the defence, sub- mitted that defendant's words did not amount to a war- ranty, and he also commented upon the contradictions in the evidence of the plaintiff and the witness Bailey. After Mr. Browne's address,without requiring witnesses for the defence, his Honour gave judgment for the de- fendant.

IMPORTANT TO PAWNBROKERS.—EIiga Smith, of Poplar House, Stockport-road, Levenshulme sued Mr. Isaac Houghton, pawnbroker, Mersey-st., for the sum of £2 10s. the value of a dress which she had pawned with the defendant and which he had lost. Mr. Browne appeared for the defendant. From the plaintiff's evidence it ap- peared that she pawned the dress for Bs. on the 20th Sep- tember, 1890, and on the 6th September, 1891, she, not being able to pay for the loan back, sent by postal order interest for the same to renew it for a further term of twelve months. Xi% Houghton sent her word that he had lost the dress and asked her for a description of it so that he might try to find it, at the same time returning the postal order. She sent a description of the dress but Mr. Houghton could not find it. Mr. Browne, for the defendant, admitted the facts but relied on the Pawnbrokers' Act and called his Honour's atten- tion to the fact that by section 25 of the Pawn- brokers' Act, 1872, a pawnbroker was only bound to deliver up an article on payment of the loan and profit, and, inasmuch as the plaintiff had only tendered interest,' he submitted Mr. Houghton was not bound to renew the contract, and was legally entitled to refuse it, which he did, and the 12 months and seven days grace which was allowed by another section of the Act, within which a Pledge might be redeemed, elapsed before any further offer was made, and as a matter of fact no offt:r has yet been made to tender or repay the loan. He further pointed out that, by section 17 of the same Act, an article which was pawned for a sum less than 10s. became the absolute property of a pawn-broker, unless it was redeemed within the days of grace.--Elis Honour, after consideration, said that he thought he shonld find for the plaintiff, inasmuch as Mr.Houghton had practic- ally told her that the article being lost it would be useless for her to offer to repay the pledge, and therefore the Act of Parliament did not apply. After hearing evid- ence as to the value of the dress his Honour gave a verdict for 35s.,less Bs. the loan, and 2s. interest, leaving the net amount of damages at 255. Mr. Browne asked that a case might be stated as it was an important matter for pawnbrokers, but his Honour declined on the ground that there was no law involved, but merely questions of fact.
THE ALLEGED MURDER NEAR WREXHAM. SUICIDE OF THE ACCUSED.

The charge against a collier named Williams of wilfully and feloniously killing a fellow-workman named Jones, has had a most startlingending, as on Monday afternoon the accused committed suicide at the Police Station, Wrexham, where he was confined, waiting to be brought before the magistrates. The prisoner hung himself with a large handkerchief, which he twisted into a rope, and then getting on the top of the heating apparatus, he placed the handkerchief round his neck and over an iron bar. Having made the handkerchief secure, he must then either hate thrown himself or slipped off the ap- paratus.

div.head: ENGLISH CHURCH UNION.
div.p: THE ENGLISH CHURCH UNION.

On Tuesday afternoon a meeting of the Warring- ton branch of the English Church Union was held at the Lion Hotel, Warrington. ' The Rev. G. D. Garvin presided, and amongst others present were the Mayor (Alderman F. Greenall), the Rector of Warrington the Rev. F. W. Willis), Rev. F. F. Slater, Rev. G. D. Wray, Rev. L. J. T. Darwall, Mr. John White, Mr. C. S. Burgess, Mr. G. J. Worley, Mr. S. Davies, &c., there being a fair attendance. In his report as Secretary, Mr. J. White referred with much regret to the recent death of Mr. Egerton Warburton, of Arley, the president of the branch, and also to the demise of the Rev. D. S. Hodgson. There, were, he said, now 83 members and associ- ates of the branch, one less than last year. While, however, the membership of the branch remained stationary, the number of those outside the ,Union who sympathised with its work continued to increase rapidly.—Mr. James Bolton, the treasurer, reported that there was a balance in hand last year of 45. 2d.;, the donations dur- ing the year had been £1 16s. 6d., and the subscriptions a 7s. ed. The balance now in hand was 6s. 2d.—On tlw proposition of the Rev. F. Slater, the report and balance sheet were adopted.—A resolution regretting the death of Mrs. Warburton having been adopted, the following officers of the branch were appointed :—Pre-ident, Rev. Canon Heron; vice-president, Rev. E. D. Garvin; hon. treasurer, Mr. James Bolton • hon. secretary, Mr. John White; committee, Rev. F. Slater, Rev. R. H. Ashe, Mr. H. N. Houghton, and Mr. C, S. Burgess.—An address was next given by Mr. Thurnham, of Liverpool. He quoted the words of the Archbishop of Canterbury to the effect that "Certain things might make it incumbent upon the Church to make her political power felt," and also the words of the Archbishop of York that the "Church of England might need to

be delivered from a Parliament as from a- Pope." It did seem to him, he said, that the time had . now come when churchmen of all shades of political opinion, and of varying shades of religious opinion with- in the church, must be prepared to stand shoulder to shoulder on every possible occasion, and especially in the great council of the nation. That was,the time had come when there should be formed a distinctively church party in the Rouse of Commons. (Hear, hear.) This party should as far as possible embrace every consis- tent loyal member of the Church of England who ie returned to the House of Commons. There should be absolutely no test in this party as regarded imperial politics, so long as a man belonged to the Church of Eng- land, and stood shoulder to shoulder in defence of church interests. If the Church of England was to be ever tied to the chariot wheel of any political party her doom in the national sense was sealed. Re should be ex- tremely sorry to see the church tied to fellowship with the Conservative party. In Liverpool the main idea of that party with regard to the church was that she was a useful stalking horse for the party. The speaker then enumerated several questions upon which an independent church- party might act as distinct from political parties.—The Rev. C. E. Elcum then gave

div.head: PROPOSED ROYAL MARRIAGE.
div.p: THE PROPOSED ROYAL MARRIAGE.

It is now generally understood that the marriage of the Duke.of Clarence and Princess Mary will be solemn- ised at St. George's Chapel, Windsor, on the 10th March. The trousseau of the bride-elect will be made wholly in England. Letters and telegrams of congratulation from all parts of the Queen's realm continue to pour into Marlborough House and White Lodge, Richmond Park, and, many dis- tinguished persons continue to personally call to tender their congratulations.

The Prince of Wales on Wednesday night presided over the annual dinner of the,Civil Service, which took place at the Hotel Metropole. In responding to the toast of their Royal Highnesses the Prince and Princess of Wales and all the Royal Family, the Prince of Wales acknow- ledged the references which had been math, to the illness of Prince George, and the bethrothal of the Duke of Clarence. kle said he must thank them for their con- gratulations upon the approaching marriage of his eldest son, an event which gave his parents and every member of his family the greatest gratification. Not the least pleasant Cifeumstance was the fact that it had received the approval of the nation. He was glad and proud to think his son married one born in this country, and who had all the feelings of an Englishwoman. With regard to Prince George, he was now in a fair way to entire re- storation to health.

div.head: GIRL DROWNED AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: GIRL DROWNED AT ST. HELENS.

On Thursday afternoon Mary Ann Tracy, 15, daughter of Patrick Tracy, Stone-st., Parr, was drowned at Blackbrook, The girl with several com- panions had been picking cind et s at Baxter's Copper , Works, and on returning had to cross the "Stinking Brook " by a plank. The wind was so strong that Tracy was blown in, and owing to the recent rains and the strong current she was carried along in sight of her companions, who saw her being rolled over and over for some distance. Sergeant Sisson and three constables got grappling irons, and grap- pled for a thousand yards from the place where she was blown in, but could not find the body. Grap- pling was continued until dusk without avail. Some years ago a man fell in the brook at this point, and was carried to Warrington by the current.
SERIOUS RAILWAY COLLISION. AT ST.
HELENS.

On Wednesday night a collision took place be- tween twp coal trains near St. Helens Junction, which resulted disastrously. Two coal trains one from Westleigh and another from Lea G:een, were being shunted from the main line between Manches- ter and Liverpool round the curve near the junction for thA Garston and Widnes line. The Westleigh train was standing on the curve when, by some misunderstanding between the signalman and the driver of the Lea Green train, the latter backed into the curve too quickly, and t he brake van came in contact with the engine of the West Leigh train with such violence that the engine and the brake van were thrown over on their sides. The brakeman, Win. Henry Astbridge, of Garston, sustained a severe cut on the head and was otherwise injured, while the engine dripers, who both came from Wigan,liad marvellous escapes. A gang of men set to work at once,but it was half- past four next morning before they had cleared the line.

div.head: CRUSHED TO DEA.TFI IN A SIDING,
div.p: CRUSHED TO DEA.TFI IN A SIDING,

On Wednesday an inquest was held at sX__llelens, before Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, at the Griffin Inn, Peasley Cross, touching the death of William Don- nelly, 30 years of age,of 45,Manor-st., Peasley Cross. The deceased was employed as a brick burner at the works of Messrs. Kurtz, and on Monday forenoon was assisting to load some bricks in railway wag- gons in a siding of the works. Some waggons were being moved in the siding, and deceased stood on the brake of one waggon whilst they were in motion. He caught against a plank near the siding and was knocked between the waggon and the wall. He was terribly crushed, and was removed to the Cot- tage Hospital, where he died during the afternoon The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death,' but recommended that the lines of the siding should be placed further away from the wall.—The Coroner remarked that if the deceased had allowed the waggon to go down the siding without riding on , the brake, he would not have been killed. He (the coroner) thought it was rather an error of judgment on the part of the deceased.

Country THE charms of country life have and for generations been described, and. Town. sung, and painted, and yet it con— tinues to happen that young men and young; women leave the country to live in towns. How is it? It is not surely all make-believe—this pro— fession of delight in peaceful occupations, pure. ; air, and pleasant:scenes. No, there is a cause for the drift of population from country to town, and that is that we are not • making the most of the land, with, as a result, a poor return in the shape of wages for agricultural workers. Englishmen as: ; well gt Irishmen love their native sod, and they, would assuredly cling to it, if they saw that, they had a fair chance in life; but with a. prospect of a miserable pittance for labour, a hovel) to herd in, and the workhoUse at the end of it all,. it is not surprising that so many of them migrate from the country to the town. Most of them bet- ter themselves from a monetary point of view, but it is often at the expense of health and of , morals ;; and, besides this, by entering the labour market, of towns they make the hard struggle there for ex- istence harder still. The Liberals as a party have seen these things for a lqng time; their remedy haft been 'in the first instance to place power in the hands oi labourers by giving them votes; and,, I secondly, by assisting them in the acquirement of land by the reform of antiquated land laws.. The Tories opposed, as long as they could, the exten-- sion of the franchise; they are opposed now to any thorough reform of the land laws; but they arer just beginning to discover—as the , lesson of the recent bye elections—that Hodge will do nothing for them if they do 119 t make an effort to do some- thing for him, Sir John GORST, as a membot of the tent Government, sees how the wind is blow- ing well enough, and he would have sails trim- med to the breeze immediately. He was doing what he could, single-handed, at -Manchester', Ql-1, Monday evening, but it was obvious that lie. WE the reverse of free in his movements. Qthing could be more satisfactory than hia statement of the difficulties of the situation. He remarked that "all the little village industries which used to give employment to almost as many men as actually worked upon the land were being undersold and driven out by the cheaper factory and machine labour of the towns." And he pointed to the fact that "the farmer tried, and rightly tried, to reduce , his labour bill as much as he conld,,and by the introduction of agricultural machinery very much fewer people were necessary to cultivate the land than were necessary 20 or 30 years ago." How odd, by-the-by, that factory labour and agricultural machinery should have so mightily increased the means of production, and Yet, while the rich are., getting richer, the poor seem to be getting poorer! But, returning to Sir JOHN Go4sT,he suggests that an effort should be made to indiice a counter- ,

_ movement of emigration from the town back

again into the country. Just the thing; but how has it to be accomplished? Country life, ordinarily so dull, is to be made brighter; and, picture it, think of it, care-laden man! "the much-abused Primrose League has been a great boon to country people in that respect." Hodge is to be brought back to his hovel and 12s. a week by the cheap feeds, cheap concerts, and cheap fireworks of the Primrose League! But, stay; there is something more : " Why should not everybody who lived in the country open his gar- den to the few people who live in the neighbour- hood of his house, and in other ways show an extended sense of hospitality." Quite so; let the people peep into Paradise, if they cannot dwell there. That surely will make them contented. And yet Sir John Gorst has his doubts, for he goes on to say there was a cry for four or five acres of land; and " if the labourers thought that they could live on the land, in Heaven's name let them try the experiment." We as Liberals, say "Amen" to this ; but we do more—we mean to insist that the experiment shall be tried. The .agricultural labourer knows this, and that is why he is voting Liberal. Ha has no faith in men who show that they have no faith in him. Lord Salis- bury suggests that it woula be Letter to amuse Hodge with a circus than a Village Coun- cil ; but Sir JOHN GORST votes for the Council. He says :—" What was wanted was village meet- ings,where all the people who were interested could attend. They could not have a much fullex public life in villages than was possible in towns. They could easily have an assembly which everyone might be free to attend, at which matters like roads and schools, and questions of sanitary re- form, and the provision of land, might all be dis- cussed by the people who were most immediately interested in them." This sounds exceedingly well; but what does it really mean? Listen to this He thought it would be quite enough if they had the power of making presentments to the County Council, or the District Council, of the particular wants of their village,and of having those presentments properly considered and properly adjudicated upon by some higher authority." That is ti say the residents of villages shall be allowed to talk; but they shall not be allowed to act! If they desire to do something, they must "with bated breath and whispered hurnblenesg "make a presentment to "oOme higher authority." This is Toryism pure and simple ; it is a new reading of the old doctrine—

"Bless the Squire and his relations, And keep us in our proper stations." But it won't do ; the people in town and country have groaned too long under the oppression of higher authorities," and—judging from the London Conference this week—have determined to look to themselves and help themselves by taking power into their own hands. They mean to have direct control of their own affairs; to break down the barriers of entail and primogeniture, and get— not free land but free access to the land. It is by solid reforms that the migration from town to country is to be effected, and not by hollow talk at hollow village meetings. The one is substance, anel the otheris shadow ; and we/kers of all classes are beginning to see" which is which."
The recent conferences in Manches- A Great Reform ter on the licensing question have

resulted in the preparation of a bill embodying the conclusions come to; and on Monday this bill was itself under consideration. it will be a surprise to those who have not given much thought to the subject, to find that it is based on the assumption that one licensed house is sufficient for every 1,000 inhabitants, which would mean for a town like Warrington, 52 licensed houses, instead of 209. The basis is by no means a new one; it is the outcome, in fact,of wide obser- vation on the part of men who may be regarded as authorities on the subject. It is proposed in the bill that Town Councils and County Councils shall be named as the licensing authorities ; but, whilst this would be a convenient arrangement, it does not seem to us that it would be a satisfactory one. These bodies are already burdened with important work; and the licensing question is far too serious a matter to be relegated, in the first instance, to any authority except one specially ap- pointed for for the purpose of dealing with it. It may be taken for granted, that "the trade" throughout the country would be solidly organ- ised, and would spend an enormous sum of money in order to secure majorities and prevent anything being done in the direction of curtailing their pri- vileges. This would mean, if in any election they were successful, that a town or county would be governed, or misgoverned, by the beer interest— not only as to licensing but practically as to all other matters. This would be too great a risk to run ; for it would be the means of displacing men who have been of great service in municipal government. Another clause directs that a p 0,1,1 shall be take- -non a requisitien signiii by one- nth of the ratepayet* and that nothing shall be done except with the consent of three-fourths of the ratepayers. Such a majority is lindoubtedly greater than is desirable, We, 'O6 OV!OPred to adrift that it would be inadtiSOro to have to act on wkat may be called the ‘“iiiateli vote " of a bare majority; but to get •o\r,e'r this difficulty it is quite sufficient to say the iimintity shall be one of two- thirds df. the rateets polling in any particular district:.

But hat of 'the Guttenberg licensing system whiCh was in)The years ago referred to in favour- • able 't'ettis by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN ? Lord M BATH has 1t giving, in the "Nineteenth Century" for Decv.nber, some account of the system as carried tr". 6 in Sweden and Norway. The results are extraordinary, and as gratifying as they ara extraordinary. Here are the details,as summariswl by a contemporary In Norway, by the operation of Acts pwsire" 1866 and 1871, public-houses have been practicany abolished in rural districts, and greatly diminished in numbers and brouszht under entiate control in the towns. Bergen, with a population of 60,000, has only 14 licensed houses, all undtr the strictest regulation. The system gives the Municipal Coun- cil the power of fixing the niunrser of licenses re- quired to meet the reasonable requirements of the public, and then of granting a monopoly to a society formed for the purpsse of undertaking the traffic, generally for a term of five years. The sharehorders in this society .are allowed to gain a profit not exeee4ing fire iper cent. on the transac- tions. The Council rerains full control over all the society's operations. Total's under 16 or 17 of ap- parent age are not permitted to be served at the bar,and no females may be employed in them. They open at eight j The morning and close at tell in the evening. Th.et) regulations apply at present only to the tragic in spirits, but it is expected that they will in the end cone into force with reference to the sale of wine and beer.

Fancy the public-houses of Warrington or St. Helens being whittled down to something under 20 in number! It might be supposed that so few houses would not result in anything substantial to the community, after paying all expenses, and -5 per cent. to tho monopolist Company ; but such supposition v7ould be wide of the mark. "In Bergen during 13 years the 5 per cent. allowed to the Company &mounted to ..1.;3,14Q. Pa the -other
oghly ;ather. uso, post'

div.head: > 1,- mot _ ,
div.p: hand, the council received £25,185 of excise duty and £5,120 of communal taxes, while the amount secured for public purposes was £78,965. In other words, the Company earned every year for the public interest a profit of 127 per cent. on the capital employed." Everybody, of course, knows that brewers make enormous profits ; but what a wonderful difference there is between these profits going into the pockets of private individuals, and into the coffers of the Town Council! Upon the Bergen basis of operations, towns like Warrington and St. Helens would be in a position to spend £s,ooo—not merely once in a generation—but £5,000 every year upon Baths, Technical Institute, Library, Museum, Art Gallery, Gymnasium, Park, or some other equally good thing. But more than all this, and better than all this, there is to be taken into account the improved condition of the inhabitants as a consequence of the red uc- tion in the number of public houses, and the better management of those allowed to exist. Bergen is described by Lord Meath as a striking contrast to our English towns, in" the absence of drunkenness, beggary, and squalid misery." In view of these facts, it appears to us that the Gut- tenberg system requires to be better known and more fully discussed. Temperance reformers in this country have hitherto given the proposal the cold shoulder; but why? That is a question which we should like to see answered; and we indulge the hope that some of our correspondents will give us the benefit of their views upon the subject.

We hold over until our next issue Mr. Pears' final reply to "Gnostic."

Speaking as Chairman of the Liberal meeting at Lymm, on Tuesday evening, Mr. John Rylands classed himself for once amongst the prophets,and predicted that Mr. Leadam would win. It is to be hoped the Tories will " make him prove his words." There is such as making events square with a pre- diction. Let the Liberals set themselves to the task with a will ; it can be done next time, if they determine that it shall be done.

Pity the Unionists are not agreed either as to a policy or statement of facts. It is often said that the Irish electors are governed by the pri3sts ; but the " Spectator" says :—" We hold, that the Irish peasantry dominate the priesthood much more than the priesthood dominate them." Perhaps it doesn't matter what the/ Unionists say ; it will bo aLi the, same when they go under at the General ~ . . Electiod:

With a view to strengthening the position of , the Bank of England, the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer proposes to raise the reserve of gold to "twenty-five millions—that is to say double the gold usually in stock. It may seem abig thing on the face of it, but when it is remembered that the wealth of England is being augumented at the rate of over 100 millions per annum, the wonder is that the bank reserve has not been increased llong ago,
iti'43il4)

The proposed change means that so much gold will be taken out of circulation ; and Mr. Goschen's idea is to cover the amount withdrawn by the issue of one-pound - notes. There are one-pound notes in use in Scotland, and there was a time when they were current in England. But having been dropped, the question is—will the revival be a welcome one ? The notes can of course be forced into circulation; but if the public don't take to them the experiment will be a failure ; An d Mr. Goscilen's name is already associated with sundry failures.

The Rev. Dr. Ferguson, speaking in Warrington on Monday, emphasised an opinion as to football previously expressed in this column ; namely,that it involves risk of disease of the heart, as a result of excitement and over exertion.. It is well that players should know this—not with a view to frightJning them, but in order that they may not "overdo it." Nature gives warning as a rule, and players who feel " out of form " should rest and recuperate. It is a mistake to play under such circumstances; for it may mean poor play, per- sonal injury, and the loss of a match.

It seems to be the thing this week to gush over the betrothal of the Duke Clarence and Princess Victoria Mary of Teck ; it's "so English you know." But to use another Americanism—" is this so ?" Not precisaly ; they were born in Eng- land; but so was Lord Beaconsfield; and John Bright said of him that he had "not one drop of English blood in his veins." And so it is with the Prince and Princess; they are Germans as to blood ; but we may wish them for all that, to " live long and die happy."

There was a stormy scene at a Jacobite meet- ing, on Monday night,when the Rev. R. C. Filling- ham, lecturing at Cambridge, admitted that the Jacobite League beliei7ed in "the divine right of kings "—or, as Pore has it—" the right divine of kings to govern wrong." But why treat such a lecturer seriously? Some lunatics are karmless. There is somewhere a lecturer who still believes that the earth is flat. Why not send him round with the Rev. R, C. Fillingham, and arrange for them giving a joint lecture—,ttiways in the same room, of course, and :::,,,vays at the same time?

Nktit is icnown as the Joint Committee on Rivers Pollution was at work, on Monday, considering what to do, and how to do it, Sir Henry Roscoe was consulted, and he advised : " First, to insist that no solid matter should be thrown into any watercouras or placed so as to fall into it ; secondly, to kisist on all manufac- turers using the best practicable means for render.% ing their effluents harmless, so as to caus., no polluti9Tl of the water into which it gowsl.. If the 4:ti is all that cn ry to trade. bperacatiticttetbnlleptemdea.nwsp.thre94dop..t,neidt; Another advantage 18 that the same will apply to sewage pollution as well as to manufacturing pollution."

There can be no question that Sir Henry Roscoe's advice is sound ; but everything turns on -what are "the best practicable means." We have in mind the trial of a river pollution case in con- nection with a manufactory at Clitheroe. The defendants pleaded that they had used the best practicable means ; but before this could be deter- mined a host of witnesses had to be examined, and there was plenty of work for lawyers. The Joint Committee will, or should, have an advantage in 'that they will appeal to local authorities to assist them. They will need to be firm impartial and energetic. They have a big job before them.

From the remarks made at the meeting of the English Church Union at Warrington, on Tuesday, it would appear that the members regard their mission as practical,y accomplished. That mission was to defend and sustain what is known as ritualism. Lord Boxonsfield, when Mr. Disraeli, brought in a bill which, he plainly said, was "to put down Ritualism." The bill was carried ; it became law ; but,instead of putting down Ritual- ism, it has been itself put down. This ought to be mentioned on Primrose Day when Lord • Beaconsfield's praises are being chanted. He must have been in the wrong, if the " E.C.U." is in the right.

There was a discussion at the Rural Deanery of Frodsham, which was held at Runcorn, on Monday afternoon. The magistrates of St. Helens had before them, on Monday, a shocking case of neglect of three children. According to the evidence" The child- ren were found to be almost covered with sores and scabs. The only furniture was an old chair and an old table, and there was not another thing in the kitchen—no cooking utensils, no crockery ware, and no food of any kind. There was no bedstead, no bedding, nor clothing, but a lot of wet and dirty straw, the smell from which was intoler- able." Husband and wife were sent to prison for fourteen days, while the children were removed to the workhouse. But when the fourteen days have elapsed, what then? The question sets one won- dering why such men and women were brought into the world?

Some time ago Mr. Gladstone remarked that the head seemed to grow after the body had arrived at maturity, as he found that a Court hat which he used to wear was now very much too small for him. It was suggested by way of explanation that, instead of the head expanding, the hat had shrunk. Mr. Gladstone now touches another interesting personal matter. Addressing the Hawarden Volunteers, the other day, he said: —" I am thankful that you have not reached the time of life which I have reached, when a man be- gins not to do, as it is hoped some of the recruits will do—to advance in stature, but when he be- gins the disagreeable process of going downwards. That is the process I have been engaged in for some years, and I have lost about two inches of the stature which I once possessed." A decline of two inches is remarkable. It accounts probably for the earlier portraits of the great statesman giving him the appearance of a person taller than the man we see to-day.

Fletcher at Widnes Petty Sessions. on Thursday, John Hoffman and Ulanna llgha, of 18, Hope-st., both Poles, were charged with stealing .-q.lO money, two quilts, and two sheets, the property of Jacob Ilgha, the hus- band of the female prisoner. It appeared that Hoffman was a lodger with the prosecutor, and on Tuesday morning when he arrived home from work he found that his wife and lodger had left the house and taken the money named. Information was given to the police, and Constable Evans went to Liverpool on Wednesday, and apprended the pri- soners at Lime-st. Station. They had booked pas- ages to America. They were remanded until Monday. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. Si; W. Durros,Sankey-street. Warrinzton.-21dvt.
MR. Moss, M.P., AND THE SALVATION ARMY DIS-
TURBANCES AT EASTBOURNE.

Mr. James Hargreaves, of Widnes, has been in- teresting himself about the Salvation Army perse- cutions at Eastbourne, and recently wrote to Mr. Moss M.P., asking him to endeavour to persuade the Home Secretary to use his influence to stop the pro- ceedings which have taken place in that town. Mr. Moss replied stating that he had received other pro- tests from Widnes respecting the same deplorable proceedings, which he had laid before the Home Secretary, and on Saturday week he called at the home Office, and was assured that Mr. Matthews had done all in his power in the matter, and several civilians were now awaiting their trial for rioting. Mr. Moss said that so long as the local law remained which forbade processions it must be obeyed. He would have great pleasure in supporting a measure with the object of abolishing that clause in the local law which has indirectly led to the disturbances complained of. He further hoped that until that could be done, both parties would assist the local authorities to maintain order, and terminate what was a disgrace to the town.

div.head: ST. HELENS RIVAL TO TOMMY BURNS.
div.p: A ST. HELENS RIVAL TO TOMMY BURNS.

Jack Dyer, c3llier, of Pocket Nook-st., St. Helens, is anxious to outrival Tommy Burns. It will be remembered that on November 7th, when the police prevented Burns diving from the viaduct bridge at Earlestown, Dyer, to the surprise of every body, unceremoniously performed the feat. He has since expressed his intention of diving from War- rington Bridge to-day (Saturday) at three o'clock, and that he is willing to do any feat with Burns. . .

UMBRELLAS itECOVERE.D.—J. and -W. DUTTON, Sallkey-St., Warrington.—Aivt. TOMMY BURNS TO THE RESCUE. On Saturday afternoon, Tommy Burns was engaged in diving feats at Garston, in the presence of a large crowd of people, who were assembled near the Custom _House. One of the spectators, who was on a steam launch, jumped into the water and although his name did not transpire, it appeared he was known as " the doctor.'' The man sank twice, and was in considerable danger of his life, as the tide was flowing very strong. Burns, after several attempts, succeeded in bringing him to the surface, and he was afterwards conveyed to the Pier Hotel, where he as treated for immersion. Burns was loudly cheered for his .gallant rescue.

A Dim IN THE VIADUCT Wong, A. strange visitor made its appearance in the Via- duct Works, Earlestown, on Monday afternoon, in the shape of a young deer. The animal had come from the Burtonwood side of the eanal,`and having swam across, mounted the steep embankment near the arches. On reaching the top, it became frigh- tened at the sight of several men, and making its way round by the wheel works, made off into the field behind Mr. Emmett's house, and taking to the water again, got into another field. When last seen it was going in the direction of Newton Com- mon. It is supposed to belong to Lord Gerard, and to have strayed from the park. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, on Mon- day held an inquest at Widnes on the body of James Gee, aged 15 years, of 15, Ilisher-st. It ap- peared titat about eight months ago the deceased was watch** some youths jumping, when one of them nameid Ralph Roscoe who was holding his cap in his hold accidentally struck the deceased on the nose with the peak of the cap. He bled profusely and had since that time suffered much pain in his nose.—Dr, Allen said he was first called to the boy on the 10th November. He discovered that there was a serious disease of the nasal bone existing internally and ,he suspected meningitis, which supposition proved to be correct. In his opinion there was something wrong with the nose previous to the injury,but he thought the blow had hastened the lad's death.—A verdict of "Accidental Death " was returned. SACRED CONCERT AT WA-BORA:CB CHURCH. On Sunday afternoon what must be termed a sacred concert was given in the Wargrave Church, by the choir, for the purpose of raising funds towards the purchase of two new stops tor the organ. About three months ago a similartoncert was given, when the sum of .ClO was raised, but on this occasion, although there was a more numerous audience, the collection only realized ..C7 4s. sd. After the congregation had sung the 84th Psalm,Mr. Leyland, played a Fantasia, in" A" flat on the or- gan,which he executed with his accustomed ability. Mr. G. Wright opened the vocal part of the prd- gramme, with the air "It is enough," from Elijah, which he sung fairly well, his opening being a trifle strained, due to the presence of a cold. Thechorus "But the Lord is mindful of his own," was the best contribution by the choir of the afternoon. The excellent balance of parts was noticeable at the opening, and this was well maintained throughout. Miss E. Davies, owing to a cold, did not attain her usual standard in 4. God shall wipe away all tears.' The duet " Come ever smiling liberty," by trebles and altos and chorus. " Lead on, Lead on," was very well given. Mr. G. Mr. Welsh quite, excelled himself in the sacred song" Lead thou me on." the extreme care,and taste with which he sub- mitted the beautiful air, being highly commendable. The air "Waft her, angels," received careful treat- ment at the hands of Mr.-Nichols, and Miss Kean gave a rich exposition of the sacred song "Calvary," the various gradations being carefully adhered to and brought out. The chorus "Sing unto God" was fairly well sung, as also was the air " Rejoiae, 0 Judah:" by Mr. Wright, and chorus "'Hallelujah, Amen." The programme was brought to a close by Mr. Leyland with an organ solo" Grand march in E , flat." ( West). Mr. Davies efficiently conducted in the choruses, and Mr. E. PLENTIFUL WATER SUPPLY: -FLOODS AT THE GAS WORKS.

The Gas Meter Committee recommended that the ten- der of Hamor Lockwood of £7OB 9s. 6d. from the engine bed at Netherley be accepted. The gas was tested on the 16th and 30th insts,and showed the illuminating power to be 1996 and 1831 candles free from sulphu- retted hydrogen. The engineer reported as follows : Flood at Gas Works—" Owing to the heavy rains on the 10th and 11th inst., the water in Bower's Brook at the Gas Works rose to within 161 in. of the flood line of November, 1886, but fortunately the rain ceased soon after the water had begun to rise in low parts of the works, and consequently no damage was dne. But for this fortunate circumstance—which my not eecur the next time—there is little doubt but that the yard would Soon have been submerged and gasmaking stopped, as -at 4 p.m., about the time the rain stopped, the water was rising above the apex of the culvert at the rate of five inches an hour. It should be clearly understood that with Bower's Brock in its present state a constant supply of gas to the town cannot be guaranteed.—sul- phate Plant—This plant has worked 26 days during the past month. No sales have been made. Present stock 50 tons. The rainfall for the month has been 2.54 inches. It was recommended that on-and after the Ist January next, the price of coke be reduced to 9s. per ton, and that tenders be invited for the erection of the new engine houses at Netherley according to the designs of Messrs. Edison and Son. The water in stockwas 8,717,541 gallons and the water delivered showed an increase of 6 per cent. The amount of gas delivered showed an increase of 14.48 per cent.—Mr. Brown moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Wright seconded the adoption of the minutes. Carried.

At a meeting of the Highway Committee on the 26th November, Mr. Sadler reported that the deputation ap- pointed at the last meeting of the Committee, and con- sisting of himself, Mr. Neil, and the Clerk and Surveyor, had kad an interview on Thursday last in London with Mr. Boweliffe and Mr. Shelmerdine, on behalf of the owners of the Leigh estate, with respect to the proposed construction of public sewers on land belonging to the estate near to Lowerhouse-lane, and the straightening and improvement of that road, and the Clerk read a minute of the terms provisionally arranged betwem the deputation and the representatives of the owners of the Leigh estate for the acquisition by the Local Beard of certain easements for the construction of sewers over portions of the Leigh estate shewa on the plan produced free of cost, the owners contributing a sum of £236 to- wards the cost of constructing the sewer between Moor- lane and Milton-road, and also agreeing to provide the neeesary land for improving Lowerhous-lane, be- tween Kelsall's corner and Birchtield-road, as propoLz:•(1 by the Local Board, the Local B3ard undertaking on the , other hand to give the owners of the Leigh estate facili- ties tor substituting a proposed. new road or roads for portions of Lowerhouse-lane, as also shewn on the plan, as and when they may desire to construct such substi- tuted road or roads. Recommended that the proposed terms be accepted and embodied in an agreement to be prepared by the Clerk.—Mr. Sadler moved the adoption , of the minutes.—Mr. Taylor seconded the motion.—ln answer to questi..)ns, Mr. Sadler said the total cost of the scheme it was estimated would be about £4,300, of which the Leigh estate would contribute £236, and also give all the necessary land .—The minutes were approved.
THE SULPHURETTED HYDROGEN NUISANCE.

The Health Committee reported that the statement of estimate and expenditure prepared in pursuance of resolutions passed at the last meeting of the Committee, showing an expenditure of £52 2. 11d, in excess of the estimated cost was submitted and considered. The Medical Officer reported that during November there were 97 births and 49 deaths being at the respective rates of 37'54 and 1898 per 1000. "One of the assist- ant nurses at the Infectious Diseases Hospital was at- tacked by typhoid fever, but is now convalescent. My attention has been called to eight backyards in Nelson- st., from 38 to 52, which were covered with stagnant water,and were remedied in a few days. I have visited the various houses where infectious diseases were re- ported, and found, as a rule, that the ashpits were too deep and soon became filled with rain water; there was no suitable drainage from them and percolation through the brickwork took place, either into the yards or the back passages. This may account for cases of typhoid or scarlet fever. I have noticed frequently during the month the streets and roads in various parts of the town- ship covered with a blueish deposit, which I attributed to the sulphuretted hydrogen escaping from the chim- neys where the Chance Claus process is carried on. On these occasions the wind was easterly, and sometimes the weather foggy. I have visited both hospitals Occa- sionally and have found the management satisfactory." —Mr. Wright in moving the minutes ; said there had been some serious escapes of sulphuretted hydrogen. The Clerk had written to the Government Inspectors and to the Alkali Company, and they had replies. The Committee were still trying to make them toe the mark. The matrons of the hospitals were wishful to give the patients a little special treat at Christmas and they hoped that if it were made known the charitably dis- posed would send se.mething for the patients in the shape of toys and books &c.—Mr. Heyes said the escape of sulphuretted hydrogen had been much worse during the past few months than ever before. He was sorry that the Committee did not get anytinearer the suppression of the dreadful nuisance.—Mr. Wright said they had very great difficulty in getting the Government Inspectors to assist them in this matter or say whfre the nuisance arose from. They were inclined to think it was not from the Chance Claus process but from the waste heaps. To do what Mr. Heyes required might result in enormous expenses and he thought the best thing would be to get-the Inspectors to be a little more stmt.—The minutes were passet

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT RUNCORN, &c.
Br AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

All things come to him who waits, it is said, and if the people of Widnes will possess their souls in patience yet awhile, they will obtain their charter of incorporation. It is twelve months since the Local Board applied to have the powers and privi- leges of a corporate borough, and nine months have elapsed since the Local Government Board Inquiry into the circumstances was held, and it was fondly hoped that the. first election of councillors could take place last November. According to latest in- formation, another year must roll before that im- portant event takes place. When in London, last week, the Clerk (Mr. Oppenheim) and Mr.S. Sadler called at, the Privy Council Office, and had an in- terview with the assistant clerk `,o the Council, who stated that it was unlikely that the charter would be granted earlier than April or May. The first election of the Town Council cannot, therefore,take place before next November.

Suitors at Widnes County Court will be glad to learn that better facilities are to be granted them. A short time ago a petition was forwarded to Mr. T. C. Edwards Moss, M.P., for presentation to the Lord Chancellor, praying that the County Court offices in Widnes might be kept open daily instead of only two days a week, and that reference books be kept there. Mr. Moss now writes to say that the Lord Chancellor doubts whether the amount of business in the Widnes office justifies the whole change de- sired. His lordship,however,intimated that instruc- tions would be given to keep the office open three days a week,and that if better accommodation could be obtained, the books might be kept at Whines instead of St. Helens.

The numerous followers of football in Runcorn are much elated at the fact that two members of the local team have been selected to represent their county in the match North and South, which takes place at Newcastle on Saturday next. Houghton, the full back, has long been marked out for high honours,and Riley is a most dashing and skilful for- ward. It is hoped that both men will justify their selection.

A great improvement is about to take place at Savages Bridge, Runcorn. Mr. P. Speuknaan, the owner of the land adjoining the Westminster Cocoa ooms, has approved of plans for erecting thereon five shops and a building for the General Post Office, and the contract for the work has been secured by our townsman, Mr. H. Coward. The design .of the buildings is of a handsome description and the ac- corao4ation most ample. The appearance of the bridge will be much improved by the structures, and the post office officials will be delighted to remove from their present inconvenient quarters.

Captain Paul, of Runcorn, has just made a very smart passage in his three-masted schooner Gleaner. On the llith November the Gleaner left Liverpool for Aviles, in Spain, and arrived back with a cargo of nuts,and docked at Liverpool on the sth inst., thus atcomplishing the out and home passage, in- cluding discharging and unloading at Aviles, in 19 days. The "Liverpool Journal of Commerce" describes this as an exceptionally quick run, In October last the vessel crossed the Atlantic from Harbour Grace to Kingroad, Bristol, in 13 days.

Owing to indisposition, Miss Annie Rich "rdson, has been compelled to cancel her engagement with the Runcorn Musical Society for the concert oq the 21st of the present month. The Committee how- ever, have been fortunate in securing the services of Miss Sarah Berry, and that lady will take the place of Miss Richardson. A native of Heywood in Lancashire, Miss Berry was discovered only a few years ago ; and gaining a scholarship at the Royal College of music, she enjoyed for a time the tuition of the late Madame Lind Goldsschmidt. Her debut was made at, one of Mr. De Jong's concerts on Jan. 7th, 1858, and her first appearance in oratorio was something under two years ago. Miss Berry is now filling engagements with all the principal societies in the country.

Runcorn Free Library Committee have decided to open the Reading Room on Christmas Day,and on Thursday the Board of Commissioners endorsed their action. This is a step iji the right direction, and no doubt many who find time hang heavily on their hands on that day,or who are away from home and friends will there spend a few pleasant hours reading the literature of the day. Perhaps the day will come when we can uso this most useful insti- tution on the day when working people have most time—and that is Sunday.

Mr. Philip Speakman, C.C., has been appointed a • member of the Committee formed in the endeavour to obtain a vehicular bridge across the Mersey. By the bye, I wonder if this project is making any progress? flow would it be to make this a "plank in the platform " in the Runcorn and neighbouring constituencies at the approaching County Council election? • 1

It is the end and aim of one class of social reformers to find a counter attraction to the public house, which in their eves is the embodiment of all that is evil and misleading. The coffee tavern' that have been established certainly cannot be described as a huge success in drawing away customers from Brother Bung, and the shareholders of our local coffee palace at the foot of Savage Bridge, are not amassing fortunes by the sale of fragrant coffee or that excellent tanning called tea, ( Vide Mr. Earp). But then that is a minor matter ; the saving of the sinner and not the making of " divi," was their motive in starting the concern.

Mr. Wm. Holt must have forgotten this institu- tion when he stated the other day that his dancing saloon was the "only place in Runcorn where young people can be kept away from the public house. He sought to obtain a license for this haven of pure enjoyment, this antidote to the publican's poison, this place where " there was no harm in the enjoy- ment." But the police held strong views on the subject, and this dancing saloon was condemned in strong language! We ought to thank the Legisla- ture for the Public Health (Amendment) Act, and our Board of Commisioners for adopting it, as by means of its pr9visions the Bench of magistrates were enabled to shut up the place by refusing license. Air. Holt must now compete with the publican in another direction.

Superintendent Noblett of Witina, has beep. i ! appointed to the important division of Bury near Manchester, in succession to Superintendent lien- derson, who has been superannuated. While glad to hear of Mr. Noblett'a promotion the people of Widnes will be sorry to lose him, as during the brief period of melve months that he has been in ,charge of the division, his sterling qualities of mind ' And heart, havt won for him the admiration and respect of all who knew him. There will be some Compensation in the fact that his place will be taken by a tried, trusted and respected officer, in the person of Inspector Keighley. Mr. Keighley has now been in Widnes for many years, and his appointment to the thief position will be hailed with satisfaction. I congratulate both officers and hope they may win further successes in their pro- fession. Sergeant Pattinson, of the Kirkham Division, has been promoted to Inspector, and comes to Widnes, with a character for intelligence and fairmindedness.

At the Petty Sessions, the magistrates (Mr. Timmis and Mr. Birchall), congratulated both gen- tlemen on their promotion and also on their long and honourable career, in the force. Superintendent Noblett has been in the force 2G years and. Superm tendent Keighley 28 years. -

Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., has purchased the Primi- tive Methodist School, in Regent-st., Runcorn, and it will now be principally used for the lodge meet- ings of Friendly Societies, or for the meetings of members of trades organisations. It is well adapted for this purpose. I alsounlerstand that " pleasant Sunday afternoon meetings" will be arranged. They will consist of lectures of an elevating ten- dency, withal entertaining and instructivv, and of musical performances, not necessarily sacred, but suited to the character of the day. It is believed , that pleasant gatherings of this description will do [ untold good.

There was quite a phenomenal attendance at the last meeting of Runcorn Commissioners. Seven- teen members were present out of a possible 'eighteen, and it is some years since there were so many present. The chief interest of the proceed- ings was in the proposed Technical Institute. A sub-committee was appointed to draw up a schedule of the requirements, and also to consult Mr. Bow- den a civil engineer, of Manchester, as to the best mode of constructing the institute. It was also decided,after a long and animated discussion, to ap- propriate the vacant land adjoining the Town Hall for the site of the proposed Institute. Mr. Prit- chard and Mr. Humphreys objected to the definite selection of this site until others had been ex- amined, but as they had nG others to suggest it is difficult to understand their position. The Town Hall site is central, easy of access, and in a quiet neighbourhood and if it meets with the require- ments of the case, no better could possibly be found in the neighbourhood. One pleasing feature of the whole proceedings was that all seemed imbued with the idea that the Institute must be worthy of the town and the object and erected as quickly as possible. The discussion was not carried on quite the recognised "Parliamentary lines." and some questions put by Mr. Meadowcroft at the close elu- cidated the term "out of order," and it is to be hoped that they will pay more regard to standing orders in future, and so expedite business.
THE NEW SEAMEN'S INSTITUTE, RUNCORN.

On Thursday afternoon, Dr. Jayne, Bishop of Chester, opened the new Seamen's Institute, which has been erected in Station-road,in connection with the Mersey Mission to Seamen. The old Mission Room at Bottom Locks had become too small for the purposes of the Mission, besides being in an in- convenient position. About .£1,600 has been spent in erecting the building,which is of the Gothic style of architecture, designed by Mr. John Wilson. It is constructed of local red bricks, faced with terracotta, and has a semi-ecclesiastical appearance. The upper room, which is to be used for religious services, is ap- proached by a flight of steps, which give a bold appear- ance to the entrance. In dimensions it is 30 feet by 65, and is provided with polished pitch pine open seats,cap- able of accommodating 250 worshippers. The roof is on the hammer beam principle. Natural light is admitted by fine tracery windows, on the south side, and one at both the east and west end. Artificial light is provided by three twelve light coronas. The appearance of the „ hall is very bright and cheerful. The lower room, which is of similar dimensions, is intended for purposes of re- creation by the sailors and boatmen of the port. News- papers, tcc., will be provided, games of various descrip- tions will be permitted,and the frequenters can also have the uninterrupted solace of a smoke. On Sundays the rooms will be used as a Sunday School. At the rear are two small rooms, one of which is fitted up as a Library and the other for a class room. There is also a boiler house, and a complete lavatory arrangement. The building is heated through by Mr. W. E. Lea's patent hot water apparatus. It only remains to say that Mr. EL Coward, the contractor, has given every satisfaction in his work.

The Mission Hall was crowded by a congregation to witness the dedication service. Besides the Bishop, the clergy present were the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, M.A., Rural Dean, Rev. Dr. Preston, M.A., Rev. W. C. Woos- nam (chaplain), Rev. J. Wilcockson, Rev. J. Fell (Liver- pool) and Rey. S. H. Fullerton (Bootle), and the follow- ing missionaries Messrs. W. Shaw (Runcorn). John Howard (Ellesmere Port), and George B. Hutton (Birken- head.)—The Rev. W. C. Woosnam read the prayers and the Rev. Canon Wood the lessons. —The Bishop preached from the words " But Jerusalem, which is above is free; it is the mother of us all," and in the course of his re- marks said they believed in one mother Church, but far be it from him to say hard words of those who differed from them perhaps through their own fault and through provocation. But still truth was truth and the Bible seemed distinctly to teach that in the household of God there should be one mother. The Church should not be a weak mother,but she could not be too sympathetic,and the Church was trying to hold out a sympathetic hand to the Seamen's Mission and Institute. It was the duty and privilege of those interested in the trade of Runcorn to take a special and liberal interest in that institution, and to help to provide for the sailors and boatmen who tended to the post. Sailors were missionaries who were continually going to foreign lands and it depended upon the training they received at home whether they were good or bad advertisements of the cause of Christianity. —The Bishop then licensed Messrs. W. Shaw, J. Howard, and G. B. Hutton, Seamen's Missionaries, as lay workers in the parish of All Saints.

In the evening a public meeting was held in the Recreation Room. There was a large audience and Dr. Jayne presided.—Mr. C. J. Bushell, president of the Mersey Missions, delivered the opening speech and com- plimented the architect and builder upon their work. That building was designed to minister to the spiritual wants of the sailors and boatpeople. Their spiritual needs would be dealt with in the church overhead. Sailors and boatmen were only human and required wholesome recreatien and there they would find it and also sympathetic friends, who would endeavour to raise them in the social scale and help them on their toilsome journey through life. (Applause.) In conclusion he thanked the people of Runcorn for the efficient help they had given to their indefatigable agent Mr. Shaw, with- out whom he did not believe that building would have been erected. (Applause).—Mr. Garrett, the hon. secre- tary to the Building Committee, read the statement of accounts showing that there was a debt of £221 ts. id. on the building, and the &MI of £4OO owing for the land. He hoped those present would give every help in clear- ing off this debt and so relieve him of his duties. They had to thank the Society for the Promotion of Christian. Knowledge for £5 worth of prayer books; vicar and churchwardens of Christ Church, Waterloo, for Com- munion cloth; vicar and churchwaidens of Willaston, for oak lectern; Miss Heyworth for a harmonium, and Mr. and Mrs. Abel for cushions. (Applause.) The Chairman said he was very deeply interested in this undertaking and very grateful he was to those who. under God had been able to carry it on to the present condition. He hoped that in the future it might be- came a source of very wide and probably unexpected blessing and helpfulness to those for whom the mission was intended. (Hear, hear.) They were deeply in- debted to those who for 14 years had laboured with so much success in this good cause. (Applause.) He im- pressed upon those present that if real results were to be achieved in this new building there must be constant earnest and prayerful effort. (Applause.) The Rev. Dr. Preston proposed a vote of thanks to the ladies who had presided at the tea tables, and in the course of his speech mentioned that his father-in-law,Mr. Philip Darbyshire,was the means of bringing the Mersey Missions into Runcorn.—The motion was carried.— Captain Crowther moved a vote of thanks to the Bishop. —Mr. W. Shaw seconded, and describing his work, said the sailors and boat people were in no one's parish; they were here to-day and gone to-morrow,but they had souls to be saved as much as the very highest man and woman in the land, and he hoped that God would enable him to lay hold of them in a humble, simple, and plain way. (Applause.) He did not want townspeople to come and fill the place upstairs, and push the sailors and boat people out. (Applause.) Most of the towns- people were settled in some place of worship, and if they were not, they ought to be. (Laughter.) He mentioned that the vicar and curates were going to help with the Sunday morning's services, and offered his grateful thanks to Mr. W. Hayes, Mr.. S. Taylor, and Mr. and Mrs. Abel for their great lielo —The motion was carried by acclama- tion.--The Rev. Hon. Grimston (Ship Canal chaplain) moved a vote of thanks to the subscribers, and the. Rev. W. C. Woosnam seconded in an earnest speech,and the motion-wa.s carried by acclamation on the proposi- tion of Mr. John Wilson seconded by the Rev. J. Holden. and supported by Captain Shaw, a vote of thanks was. tC accordedchair- when i.,i to s lordship the Canon elohV s, t rawho n took—lh the p icyhiahi; the Vicar pointed out that the services of the Church of Englano were not of the stereotyped style that many people imagined and indi2mted the idea that churchmenk when they prayed could not do so outside the backs of the prayer book. It was a common error to suppose that because laymen did not take part in the services. in church therefore they could not be recognised as church workers if they would undertake to find an earnest man desirous of doing spiritual work not for his own glory but for the glory of God—they would. undertake to find him work to do. Alluding to the ha rd lot of the working classes, the Vicar said excuses could be made for them not attending church and if they had t to get them to worship they must give them a service of such a character that they would feel that it had been good for them to be there. This was one reasola, why be welcomed such places as that mission.
The collections amounted to £22 es. ()id., including a cheque for £lO from Mr. Tom Mathieson.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
THE "ALLEGED WOUNDING WITH A KNIFE."

In this police case in which Mary Ellen White and Jane Cook summoned each other for assault, it was by an in- advertency in one passage in our report, made to read that Cook accused White Gif wounding her with a knife, and of taking advantage of her being in the Infirmary to get out her summons first. As the context of the re- port stated it was Cook who was thus charged by White. It was White not Cook who was wounded and had to be conveyed to the Infirmary.

div.head: EXPOSING BAD MEAT FOR BALE.
div.p: EXPOSING BAD MEAT FOR BALE.

At The Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday, Wm. S. Banks, butcher, of 6, Buttermarket-street, was charged with exposing for sale, on Wednesday last, three pieces of mutton, weighing 161b5., unlit for human food. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, town clerk, appeared for the prose- cution, and asked for a severe penalty. Mr. Norman, inspector of nuisances, proved the case, and deposed to seizing the meat and conveying it to the Town Hall, where it was seen by Alderman Harrison and ordered to be destroyed.—The defendant's agent said he was going round the shop to examine the stock when Mr. Norman came, and had he been there a quarter of an hour sooner, he would have ordered it to be taken away. The bad meat was all hanging by itself in one part of the shop.—Mr. Norman said this was correct.—Alderman Francomb said that was, in the defendant's favour, because to pass off bad meat a little judicious mixing would be advisable.-40s. and costs.
A RAID ON MARGARINE DEALERS.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday morning, T. H. Goodwin & Co., carrying on business as the Danish Dairy Co., Bridge-street, were charged with supplying, on the 10th of November, a pound of butter not of the nature, substance, and quality of the article demanded, also with exposing for sale on the same date a quantity of the same article, margarine, without hav- ing the nature of the article denoted thereon. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, town clerk, appeared for the prosecution, and Mr. Unsworth for the defence, Inspector Norman and Sub-Inspector Powell proved the cases, Powell stating that he purchased the pound of " butter " for Is. id., the price of ordinary cheap butter being Is. 3d. per pound. There was nothing on the wrapper or what it was taken from to show what it was. The article was certified by the borough analyst as margarine. After the purchase the defendant admitted the article was a "mixture," and wanted to put a margarine cover on it. —Mr. Welsh, manager for the defendants, said he told the inspectors twice, before the purchase, that the arti- cle was" the finest mixture." The lad put it in plain Raper by mistake, and when witness was putting the right paper on it, the inspector snatched the article away before he could do so. He admitted that the mixture was not marked as required by the Act, but said that was because they were cleaning the shop. The shop-boy having given evidence, the defendants were fined 40s. and costs in the first case. and 20s. and costs in the second.—Sarah Ann Robinson, Chorley-street. James Evans, Bridge-street, and Ann Williams Aikba-street, were fined 10s. and costs each for like offences.
A SUSPICIOUS CHARACTER AND A THEFT OF TOBACCO.

At the Warrington borough police court, on Thursday morning, Thomas McHugh, of no settled residence, was charged that he being a convicted thief, was found fre- quenting Buttermarket-street with intent to commit a felony on Thursday morning. The Chief Constable saii that on Wednesday night and Thursday morning the prisoner was seen in the street, and on Thursday morn- ing it was found that a brick had been taken out of the premises of Mr. Mee, tobacconist; at the corner of Crop- per's Brow, and tobacco to the value of 6s. Bd.—P.C. Hollingworth said alocut a quarter to eleven on Wednes- day night in Buttermarket-street he saw the prisoner coming down Town Hill with a quart bottle containing beer. He asked him to drink out of the bottle, stating that he he was going to start for Manchester. He then went away. Witness was passing Butterinarket- st. and heard a policeman's whistle, and, going in the direction whence the sound came, foundr.C. Smith in front of Mee's, the tobacconists. A brick which had been taken out of the wall was lying in the window amongst pipes and cigar holders. Witness brought In- spector Cox, who asked him if he had seen anybody about likely to do this. He told him he had seen Thomas McHugh, and while he was talking to Inspector Cox, McHugh walked up to them, and said he bad walked six miles on the way to Manchester and come back. It was then about five minutes to three. He was quite dry, though the night had been wet and stormy. It was dis- covered that a quantity of tobacco had been stolen from Mee's.—P.C. Hardy deposed to seeing the prisoner hang- ing about in the neighbourhood over night.—The Chair- man asked the prisoner how he kept dry if he had been six miles on the road to Manchester. Did he walk be- tween the spots of rain P--The prisoner could give no explanation.—He pleaded not guilty but was bound ever in the sum of £lO to appear again when called upon.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
MONDA.Y.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall), and
Aldermen Fran-comb. and Harrison

ABSENCI FROM MILITARY TRAINING.—Robert BUMS was charged with being absent from the Royal Lanca- shire Fusiliers, during their training at Bury in 1891. —The defendant said he was absent through illness from heart disease, and defective sight. He was fined 40s. and costs. BREACH OF THE EDUCATION CT.—Thomas Jones was charged under a warrant with not sending his child regularly to school. 55., and the cost of the warrant. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. —Charles Byfield, in Butter- market-st., on Saturday night, fined ss.—Ann Lins- dale, in Sankey-st.' the same night in the same street. The defendant had assaulted a boy, who was bleeding, and then pursued him. It took three constables to hold the prisoner and get him into the cells, and he made a rush at one of the constables at the station. He was -fined ss. and costs.—Sarah Williams was charged with being fo drunk and disorderly in Knutsrd-rd.' on Sunday morning, about half-past three. She had to be brought in a handcart- to the station, and she said it was because she had rheumatics, and could not walk.— Alderman Harrison: Pity but, you had rheumatics in your tongue. ss. and Costs. DRUNK.—Patrick Cullen, drunk in Winwick-rond, on the 27th ult. Fined 3s. 6d. FlGHTlNG.—Frederick Mason and Henry Beach for fighting in Buttermarket-st., on the night of the 27th ult.' bound over in £b for six months and to pay 7s. ,costs each.

OBSTRUCTION BY PERAMBULATORS.—Maggie Cowie, a little girl, was charged with obstructing the footpeh in Bridge-st., by allowing a perambulator to stand thereon on the sth inst. The Chief Constable said he had many complaints about obstruction of the footpaths especially with perambulators, and the police would have to do something in the matter. People would have to be warned not to bring perambulators out into the Market Place and the crowded streets on Wednesdays and Saturdays. There would be an accident through them some day. The defendant was dismissed with a cautim. CRIMNEY ON FIRE.--John Keith, for this offence on the 28th ult., was fined
TUESDAY. - Before Capt. Nicholson_ (chairman) and
Messrs. E. J. Guest and R. Garnett
DIDUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Thomas Henry Conroy, in Florsemarket-street, the previous day, 53. and costs ; and Thomas Collins, on Monday night, in Dial-street, ss. in- cluding costs.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Councillqr John Fairclough, (chair- man), Captain Nicholson, and Alderman Wright. Ways ASSAULT.—John Clare, labourer, Elhs-st., was charged with assaulting his wife, Hannah Clare, on the sth inst.—The complainant said he came home in drink, and kicked her several times. She took her daughter to bed with her that sight thinking thus to prevent him from molesting her again, but he compelled the daughter to go to another bed, and then pulled the complainant out of hers. She then went to her daughter's bed and he pulled her out of that. She afterwards lay on the sofa and he pulled her off that and threw alug of water over her.—The defendant, in answer tl the Chairman, said he had nothing to say.—The Chairman: Nothing to all this! —The defendant: No sir.—The Chairman said he had known the defendant a great many years, and he was a very decent man when he kept from drink.—The com- plainant : There are two things I want him to do,to keep his hands off me and to work.—ln reply to the Chairman, the complainant said she would like a separation order.— The Chairman: I know you have been keeping yourself and the family, and he has been helping to spend the money.—The defendant, who had, about 12 months asp, been bound over for assaulthig his wife, was sent to jail for 7 days; and his wire was granted a separation, her hbsband being ordered to allow her _los. a week,

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. —THB NOTORIOUI BODELIA AGAlN.—William Farrell, John O'Neil. and Bodelia Knockton, were charged with being drunk and disorderly on Town Hill, at 20 minutes to 12 the previous night.-- They all pleaded guilty.—Farrell and Knockton were fined 10s. and costs each, in default 14 days; and O'Neil was fined 55., in default 7 days.

TRuRSDAY.—Before Captain Ridgeway (chairman) Councillor James Fairclough, and Alderman Sutton. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Reid, in Buttermar- ket-st., ss. and costs.—Thomas Mitchell. in St. James's- St., the same night, 53. including ciasts. Scaoor. CASKS.—George Clements, pensioner, Phi tip- st., for not sending his child to school, had an attendance order made against him, and was fined ss. Richard Newton, brewer, William-st., 2s. 6d. William Crank, labourer. 32, Aiken-st., had his son committed to Father Nugent's school. James Lester. slater, Twiss yard, Wm. Dagnall, forgeman, 16, Warburton.st., George Harper, labourer, 14, Cambria Place, William Riley, labourer, 16, Turner-st., George Travers, hamper maker, 15, Town Hill, lnd Charles Campbell, labourer, Bakehouse Yard, ss. each. The case of George Povey, boilermaker, 10, Brackley-st., was dismissed, on his wife promising to send their son regularly to school. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. John White (chairman), Alderman Harrison and Wright, and Dr. Gornall'.

NON`-MAINTENANCB OF CHiLD RION. —Jam Cs Painter,Thos. Bailey, Richard Ridgway Samuel Beckett, and Alfred Barker, were charged by Police-Inspector James with non- contribution for the maintenance of their sons on board the "Clio."—William Moran was surnmoned for non-con- tribution for support of his son in St. Anne's Industrial School.—An order of commitment to prison for 14. days, was made against each of them, in case of their not pay- ing the arrears in a week. R.S.P.C.A. PnoszeurioN.—The following persons were prosecuted by Inspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A. Patrick Colbert. of Widnes, was charged with cruelly torturing on the Ist inst., a horse by travelling it while in an unfit state, and James Lees, cab proprietor, of Widnes, was charged with allowing the same to be so travelled.—Mr. Knowles, of Widnes, appeared for the defence.— Colbert was mulcted in the costs, and Lees fined 10s. and costs.—Alfred Trowbridge,"ryldesley, was charged with travelling a horse while in an unfit state, on the Ist inst., and Daniel Oliver, of-Tyldesley, was charged with allowing it to be so travelled. Trowbridge was ordered to pay the costs and Oliver fined 103. and costs. —Joseph Chadwick, Froghall-lane, was charged with' travelling a horse while in an unfit state, at the War- rington horse fair, and was fined 103.' including costs.— John Joseph Jackson, of Bedford Legh, charged with travelling a horse in an unfit state, was fined £1 and costs. —John Broadhurst,jun., Bewsey-road,was charged with cruelly ill-treating a horse by allowing it to be ridden while in an unfit state, at Warrington horse fair. 10s. and costs.—James Bates, Stamford-st., similarly .charged, as to the same occasion, 2s. 6d. and costs.— John Wall, Northwich, was charged with allowing a horse to be worked while in an unfit state, at the War- rington cow fair, on the 30th ult. He was fined £l, and 15s. costs.—Joseph Chapman, of Knutsford, for cruelly treating a horse, at Warrington horse fair, by beating it, 10s. and costs, £1 3s. in all. CHARGE OF ASSAULT.—John McDougall, Florence-st., was charged with assaulting Frances Agnes Green, of that street on the 4th inst. The case was dismissed.
WIFB DESBRTION.—Giorge Hazeldine was charged with deserting Elizabeth Hazeldine, his wife. The case was settled between the parties,by the defendant paying 3s. ad. costs.

A SUNDAY Ntairr Row.—Jonathan James Finch,Alfrerl Finch, and Samuel Thompson, was charged with assault- ing and beating on Sunday night, Robert Alexander Naylor, employed by his brother, a confectioner, who lives in Stamford-street.—J. J. Finch pleaded guilty,and the others not guilty. Mr. Browne appeared for the prosecution. After a good deal of evidence had been heard, Thompson was dismissed and Finch bound over in, the sum of LS to keep the peace for six months.
WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Lieut.-Colonel Gaskell.
DRUNKENNESS. —John Doyle, John Goulding, Charles McAnaspie, and J. Smith were each lined for this offence.
DEsERTEL—George McVickers was charged with deserting from the 93rd Highlanders, and he was handed over to an escort.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. DIIIRSDAY.—Before Sir Thomas Earle and Mr. J. . Fletcher.
DamironiwEss.—Sarah Walsh, Water-st., James KBla- lea, Water-st., Elizabeth Bushell, Beamont-st.; and Joseph Crompton, Farnworth, were each fined for drunk- enness.
SCHOOL BOARD CASES.—Mr. Denby, clerk to the School Board, summoned twelve parents for not sending their children regularly to school and the tsual -fine of ss. was imposed in each case.

MISCELLANEOUS.—WID. Whitlow and Thos.
