div.head: GREAT MINING DISASTER IN FRANCE.
div.p: GREAT MINING DISASTER IN FRANCE.
76 LIVES LoST

An explosion of firedamp occurred about twelve o'clock on Sunday, in one of the pits belonging to the St. Etienne Colliery Company. It has been ascertained that the dead number 76. The district is simply over- whelmed by the magnitude of the calamity, and on all sides there is evidence of the deepest and most active sympathy with the berea,ved families. Such inquiry as has been made up to the present by mining officials on the spot has disclosed gross and culpable negligence on the part of those responsible for the good working of the Ponape pit, it being clearly established that the ventilat- ing machinery was not started on Sunday morning until eleven o'clock, after having been stopped early on Saturday afternoon. It will, therefore, be readily under- stood that the vast accumulations of gas had taken place, and that explosions were simply inevitable once the shift got into full operations.

div.head: DEATH OF DOM PEDRO.
div.p: DEATH OF DOM PEDRO.

The ex-Emperor of Brazil, wile has been suffering for some time at the Hotel Bedford, Paris, developed serious symptoms at seven o'clock on Friday evening. The fever became ibtense,and Dr. Charcot was at once summoned. Nothing could be done, however, and the ex-Emperor died at five minutes past twelve, surrounded by all the members of Jai?

The sad intelligence of the death of Dom Pedro de Alcantara, ex-Emperor of Brazil, has been received with regret in Europe. Dom Pedro 11. was a student even more than a ruler. Nothing was more remarkable than the assiduity with which he devoted himself to the ac- quisition of knowledge of men and manners, and art and literature. The high culture of the late Emperor and his simplicity of tastes caused him to be everywhere regarded with the utmost respect. The-greatest domestic reform connected with his reign—the abolition of slavery in Brazil—was perfected in 1889. This excited considerable dissatisfaction amongst the planters, and was probably one of the causes of his overthrow. He visited Europe for medical.treatment again, in 1886, and three years after the revolution broke out which deprived him of his throne. After the death of his wife, which occurred in Portugal, in 1889, Dom Pedro lived in retirement in France. The funeral obsequies of Dom Pedro, ex- Emperor of Brazil, held at Paris, on Wednesday, were of a most impressive character.

div.p: RUGBY.

WIDNES Y. Mumocizi " A" THAMS.—Phyed at Wid- nes. The visitors kicked off, and play during the first half was of a give-and-take nature,no score being made. The second half opened in favour of Widnes,. and before play had been resumed many minutes, Owen scored a try, which Foster failed to improve. Alt more open game was now played,and Schunan placed the ball over once more, which, however,- was not improved upon. The game was now confined to omidfield, but with passing and a smart run,- ttushton again placed the ball over the line, the kick at goal being futile. Play con- tinued amongst the Widnes teatu,and it was quite evid- ent that their opponents were no match for them-when the whistle blew for time the score being—Widnes, 3 tries ; Tuebrook, nil. WARRINGTON 2ND V. Fucosirm ST.—The Warrington- ians journeyed to Frodsham on Saturday, the village club being met in favourable weather. Winning thstoss the homesters consented to play up the slope, and Warburton commenced, the venue being the Irrodsham quarters. The attack was maintained, Rowe being especially conspicuous and unfortunate in not scoring,. being hauled down on the line repeatedly. Ilowevn, after ten minutes' play,the defence was. broken through;. and a display of passing between Lawless and Rowe culminated in Plinston effecting a fine run in, Warburtoa. failing at the difficult place. Nettled by this reverse, the- Cheshire men attacked, and almost effected the downfall' of Warrington's goal. J. Johnson dribbled finely, but the effort came to nought, and when the- interval arrived the visitors were a try and two minors- to- nil. Restart- ing,. the Warringtonians were placed on their mettle, and their goat VMS at once placed in jeopardy. Scrambling play was the order, the monotony being relieved by Plinston,.a fine run along touch ruling the. game at half way. Frodsham, however, would not be denied, and as a result of another combined attack,. the villagers equalized, and a goal being placed from the-try, Frods- ham in the end won a well-contested game,,by a goal and four minors to a try and three minors.

WARRINGWON " T. TYLDESLEY " Tyldesley, Warrington started the game, Hampson, Lawless, and Bailey speedily taking the leather to the home 25)„ where, after some scrimmaging, Antrobus threw to, Potts, who ran in splendidly- right under the posts, Sampson kick- ing a goal. This early reverse roused the home- team, and they at once imparted some unnecessary roughness into their play, and. although Sampson kicked finely, the pushing tactics adopted forced the game on to the visitors'lines. A screw scrimmage, headed by Lawless, Davies,. Hampson„ and Phillips, saw the ball taken grandly in the lbose to the' home quarters, but a, kick being charged,.the advantage was lost. Barnes,. Row- lands, and Warburton retaliated, and the situation was further enhanced by the dashing efforts of Daniels and Forster. Hambleti was called upon hereabouts' but he cleared wonderfully well. A bad piece of play lost the ground, and Warrington were penned for some time, until Daniels, by a very smart bit of work, reached mid- field. Some -capital passing between Lally, Antrobus, Daniels, and Potts then put a different complexion on the state of affairs, and Phillips had hard lines in not scoring, a minor resulting. Although Barnes was con- spicuous on the drop out by good play, the leather was quickly hovering round Harnblett, who cleared splen- didly, the result being that Rowlands, Hampsom, Phillips and Warburton, by dashing loose play, conveyed hostilities to the line. Daniels and Potts relieved a slight pressure,. and Sampson putting in a long kick floored Wilson on the line before he could relieve, and Bailey dashing up scored far out. The drop out was returned by Lally, bat Hamnett was called up directly after, and he punted well down the field, Barnes, Law- less, Forster, and Davies carrying the game to the line,. and half time arrived with Warrington 1-1-1 to nil: Upon the resumption, the, kick was charged, and Row-- lands, Warburton, Lawless, and Phillips were notable in their endeavours by forcing Tyldesley to defend. Antra- bus ran very well to the-line, and some further attempts, at passing were again nipped in the bud, and Tyldesley were decidedly lucky in escaping with a minor. War- rington were playing finely, the smartness of the for• - wards quite upsetting the botnesters, and the conse-- quence was that some .passing between Lally, Antrobus, Daniels, and Potts enabled the latter to get another dashing try, Sampson placing a magnificent goal off touch. Another fine display of loose work headed by Barnes, Bailey, Forster, and. Rowlands, was seen, and Potts, taking the leather at full speed, dashed to the line, a minor being allowed. Tyldesley again attacked, and at length a minor was. conceded. After the drop out Lawless by following upgained a lot of ground, and a quick dribble by Phillips, Efampson and Warburton saw- the home team defending and getting a minor. The light was getting very bad, but amid some loose encoun- ters Sampson dropped a fine goal, and Warrington retired winners by to 1 minor.

div.head: TUEBROOK T. WIDNES.
div.p: TUEBROOK T. WIDNES.

Played at Tuebrook on Saturday afternoon, in fine weather. Eccles kicked off for Tuebrook. No return was made, but the Widnes forwards brought the ball back on the loose. Cooper recovered with a sprint,and the forwards, headed by Bleasdale, dribbled into the, Widnes quarters. Drummond saved pluckily by falling on the ball, and a pack resulted near the line. Bleasdale got the ball from the "heel out," and gave it to Quine, who dropped over the line near the posts, and Eccles kicked a goal from the place. Barber kicked off again from the centre. The Widnes men pushed the ball near to the line, and,after a short dribble,Hardman picked up and scored a try. Btennares attempt at goal failed. Hol- loway got the ball from a line out and passed to Eccles, who,with a smart run and kick, took play again to the Widnes end of the,field. Fletcher picked up and ran over and E. Pearson kicked an easy goal from the place. The whistle then blew for half-time, the score then being Tuebrook 2 goals (10 points), Widnes 1 try (2 points): Lyons restarted for Widnes in the second half. No re- turn was made, and the scrimmages was formed in Tue- brook's half. The homesters brought the ball up the field with a smart dribble, and Morris did good service with a fine sprint. The hornesters again got way on the loose, and took the ball to the Widnes goal line. Bren- nan cleared with a punt into touch. The game towards the end was a very fast and even one and Widnes were unable to score. Final' result—Tuebrook 2 goals (10 points), Widnes 1. try and 3 minors (2 points).

div.head: RUNCORN v. BROUGHTON RANGERS.
div.p: RUNCORN v. BROUGHTON RANGERS.

The first fixture this season between these two clubs was played at Runcorn on Saturday, the home team be— ing short of seven men,who were playing for Cheshire at Birkenhead against Durham. The visitors were fairly represented. Runcorn started, and no return being made, a scrimmage ensued in the visitors' half. From here the visitors dribbled grandly to the home line, but Evans relieved. Chapman eventually got away with a dribble' and scored a try. The kick at goal, however, failed. On re-starting,the visitors pressed aud Chapman, receiving a grand pass from Wall, had hard lines in not scoring. Several scrimmages followed, and eventually. a free kick was given to Broughton Rangers for off side by Runcorn, which slightly relieved. Medley and Fleet were subsequently responsible for Runcorn being placed on the defensive, and eventually the ball was touched. down to save disaster. On dropping out, Runcorn car. ried play to the visitors' lines, but the superior play of the Rangers' forwards soon neutralised matters. Chap- man got away with a dribble, and was only prevented from scoring by PPndlebury, when close to the home line. A minor having being registered by Runcorn, May was awarded a penalty kick, which, however, failed. The score at half time was—Broughton Rangers one try and one minor, to Runcorn one minor. On changing ends, the visitors carried the ball to the home line, when it was touched down by Runcorn. May relieved, some pressure, and in turn Robinson was called upon to save a rush, which he did smartly. 19uncorn kept up the pressure, and were awarded a minor. May eventu- ally got possession in midfield, and after a dodgy and brilliant run scored a try under the posts. The same player kickeda goal. Runcorn kept up the pressure, and were awarded a second minor. Hurst saved a dan- gerous rush by the home forwards, and ran to the home line, but was brought down by Woods. Runcorn now had slightly the best of the game, and eventually Pen- dlebury crossed the line amidst cheers, the kick failing. Runcorn maintained the supremacy until the close of the game, when the score was Runcorn one goal, one try, and two minors, to Broughton Rangers one try and two minors.

div.head: WARRINGTON V. 'TYLDESLEY.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. 'TYLDESLEY.

The fact that Buff Berry and Smack Bate, the two rival county half backs, would oppose each other at Wilderspool on Saturday, was sufficient inducement for the large crowd to turn out to witness the first match of this annual contest. Since Tyldesley won the West Lancashire Cup, they have figured on the Warrington' card ; but of all the matches played, Saturday's game will stand out prominently. The match was marked by brilliancy throughout, and although Warrington won, praise is due to the losers for their display. NY ar- rington were minas 11. The share following up of Jolley, Holmes, and Handles baffled the return, but from a line-out, Bandies passed wildly, and Shaw taking advantage of a plea of hands, placed his side on the aggressive with a huge kick. Berry, who was acting more as three-quarter than his usual position got away, but knocked on when getting into his stride, but Evans neutralized this with a fine run and kick. The two Bates passed neatly,but still no impression was made on either defence, and Boscow never failed to respond to the numerous calls made on his services. Buckley and Turner dribbled past Shaw, and Fearnley saved, whilst Taylor adopted similar tactics in response to a movement by Holmes. A wild pass by Hansom endangered the visitors' goal, but Berry made amends for the disappointment ' when he passed to Shaw, relief being promptly forthcoming. Sutcliffe came through

div.p: THE FIGHTING IN CHINA.

A telegram received in Paris from Pekin states that the Imperial trr:ops have gained a complete victory over the 'Chinese rebels in the district of the Sien Tchan,g after two day's fighting. The thorough dispersion of the in- surgents is considered to be only a question of time.

Early on Wednesday morning, at theFlaigh Moor seam of the Wheldale Coal Company, near Castleford, York- shire, a fire broke out in the pit before the general body of miners entered the pit for their daily labours. For- tunately, only about twenty men weredown in the mine at the time, and of those all are rescued but five, and these have perished.
LORD RUSSELL AND TIM GIRL WILLIAMS.

A Press agency learns that a demand has been made upon Lord Russell for a public retractation of the alle- gations made against the girl Williams ho the hearing of the Russell matrimonial suit last week, and ample com- pensation for the injury done. Failing this an action is threatened, with damages laid at R... 10,000. Mrs. Wil- liams was foster mother to Lord Russell', and vibe* she and her husband took charge of the house at Tedding- ton it was stipulated that their two daughters should be housemaids. There were •no other servants. It is alleged by friends of the family that the youngest daugh- ter became engaged to Lord Russell, and it is strongly denied that any misconduct such as that described took place between them. The girl declares that on one oc- casion she was compelled to fly from Lord Russell to her mother's protection. She and her parents were then dismissed, and they claimed compensation for dismissal. Lord Russell paid £5OO, as the Williams's allege, on account of the dismissal, on condition that the daughter brought no action for breach of promise. The girl says she received no money.
MR. GLADSTONE AT NORTHAMPTON.

Mr. Gladstone left Court Hey on Monday, and took train for Althorp Park, Lord Spencer's country seat. Mr. Gladstone was presented on Wednesday at North- ampton Station, while on his way from the residence of Earl Spencer to that of Earl Rosebery, with addresses from the Northampton Corporation and the Liberal and Radical Association. To the first he expressed his grati— fication at seeing generally the most able men in local communities taking upon themselves important public duties without fee or reward. To the second he said he looked back on a very long life passed in a. period full of interest and of benefit to the country.. He hoped the next fifty years would be equally happy, prosperous, and fruitful of good. All sorts of rumours were heard as to the parliamentary bill of fare for next session. First we were promised by the Tories and Dis- sentient Liberals local' government for Ireland. That was shunted, and then aßill was suggested to give the rural labourer command of land. Next came an almost incredible rumour that that also was to be shunted for a quack measure to introduce one pound notes. But whatever was the issue, they as Liberals would stick to their priuciples.

div.head: RURAL REFORM CONFERENCE.
div.p: RURAL REFORM CONFERENCE.

On Thursday afternoon, a conference on rural, reforms wrs held under the auspices of the National Liberal Federation, at the Memorial Hall, London. Dr. Spence Watson, who presided, said the Conference was the natural consequence of the battle which the Liberals had fought for the extension of the franchise,. and the immediate object was to obtain for agricultural commu- nities full and free voice in their own government. Mr. Joseph Arch, said what was wanted was patience and perseverance„ and he was confident that conference would result in the freedom of thousands of men and the comfort of thousands of women and children. Sub- sequent speakers advocated compulsory leasing of' allotments, the amendment of the Ground Game Act so as to enable farmers to catch vermin in the best way they could, the establishment of parish councils, the popular control of schools, reform, in the system of poor- law relief, state pensions for the aged and infirm, the progressive taxation of incomes, and the nationalisation of land. A resolution was unanimously carried, express- ing hearty satisfaction that the Liberal party was earnestly addressing itself to the improvement of the condition of the rural population, and trusting legislation would follow in the next Parliament.

The seven League games that were down for disposal *laded much as was anticipated. In five cases the home side were victorious, whilst the match at Ewood Park ended in a draw. Bolton Wanderers- are still at the head of the poll, as they sent the Wolverhampton men back beaten by three goals to nothing. This was largely due to the improvement in the play of Cassidy, cestre forward. Everton began so well at l3lackburp, bookling two goals in ten minutes, that they should have won, but the Rovers afterwards played far better. Douglas', who look the place of M'Keown at full-back, was little' use. Howarth, late of the North End, assisted Evarton as a professional for the first time, but he did not do wonders. The goal keeping of bah Arthur and Willsams was excellent.

Prestbn North End have now won sever. League fix- tures right off the reel. Their friends are hoping that they 'will again earry off the championship. To beat Derby County on their own ground was a very credit- able performance.- Burnley went down•badly at Perry Barr, D*wen were.routed at Stoke, And Accrington had the worst of matters, at West Bromwich. The three Lancashlre clubs onlY scored two goals, whilst‘ they lost 14. Notts were sadly overplayed by Sunderland, Who have novra record elipal to any team in the Leave.

Deprived,as they were of the services of Denaldson and Hood, Newton Heath stint believed themselves capa- ble of knocking out Blackpook in the F.A. cup tie lltst they were ridely awakened. The seasiders played)very smart football, and beat the Heathens by four te-three. When last at the Hyde-Toad enclosure, Blackpool drew with their opponents, sethat Newton Heath should'.inow hold them in sigh respect.

div.head: RtGßr..
div.p: RtGßr..

The unsportsmanlike conduct ce Kendal Hornets was, the means of spoiling what would have been a very at— tractive fixture on Saturday between Lancashire and Westmoreland, It is not often that a county match is upset by the act:en of one club, and the fact is to be- deplored. Two reasons are put forward for the attitude, ef the Hornets. One is that they were dissatisfied with the treatment they had received at the hands of thee Westmoreland AEsociation,t and, another is that they were xious to turn OW/ their full team in their North-west - ern League fixture at Ulverston. If the latter is the real excuse the Hornets must have-been disappointed on Saturday, as they failed to beat Ulverston. They robbed many hundreds of the pleasure of seeing an interesting county game at Whalley itange,andwbtchever way their policy is looked at it occasions general regret.

After the good display;of Dorham against Yorkshire they were largely fancied for their fixture with Cheshire ,t)111 Saturday, but luck,was dead, against them. To be beaten by a goal and a try•to a couple- of tries was un- fertunate. The play °Mlle visitors was of a fluctuating description. At times their passing was almost per- fection, and at others the •• display of the backs was xlevenly. Alderson VWS hardly so, brilliant as usual; still he was the shining light on.his side. He is sure to ray Marsh. the Swintonian, hard for the North v. South match. Houghton's dispJlay at full; back was almost faultless, whilst Crompton was• often of great service. Thertry he scored was a very clever piece of work. The Cheshire forwards were— not nearly so smart as the Northerners, who, by the.- way, only numbered fourteen

The judgments on the great matchbetween Lancashire and Torkshire have been very edifying reading. There is a pretty unanimous consensus of opinion that York- shire, were far from satisfied with the result. They hoped: to win by such a .margin that their superiority would be undeniable, instead or which they had to rest content with a lucky goat.

Wigan may be said to have been blessed with luck to dispose ef Oldham. It Was- all owing to better place kicking, Wigan turning their only try into a goal, whilst two attempts by their antagonists were failures. Halifax were successful against the-Hornets at Rochdale. Not a point could be obtained in the game between Leigh and St. Helens Recreation, Colpe,the county full back, being often conspicuous for his safety. St. Helens were only a try too good for Morecambe. That was a curious con- test atßatley, Bradford haying their lines crossed as many as four times, whilst. thebest they could do was to drop a couple of goals and run in one. try. They thus won by ten points to eight--.a narrow escape for York- shire's crack club.
DEATH OF MR, R.. E. EGERTON- WA. RE U ETON.

Mr..R. E. Egerton-Warburton died at his resi- dence? Arley Ball, shortly, after eleven o'clock on Sunday morning. The deceased,. who. had attained the advanced age' of 87 Teams, having been born in 1804: was probably the senior representative of the old Cheshire families, and was exceedingly well- known and respected. He was, educated at Eton and Oxford, and was a Justice of the Peace and Dcputy. Lieutenant for the county of Chester. In hie Obitlier days he was a prominent figure in the hunting field, all-dill,' bright and vivacious hunting songs have gained world-wide populaiity. For several years he has been totally blind, but his bodily health has been well maintained until the last few months. Colonel Piers Egerton-Warbur- ton, JW., of The Dene, Great B'udworth, succeeds to the eetates.

div.head: TIIE- FUNERAL.
div.p: TIIE- FUNERAL.

The funeral of Mr. M E. Egerton Warburton, of Arley, Hall, took place--on Thursday, at Great Bud- worthQ. About 120 tenants headed the procession, and the bier, draped with n white pall, having a large scarlet cross upon it, and covered with wreaths of lilies, was wheeled by labourers on the estateover the two and.a half miles intervening be- tween Arley Hall and Great Budworth Church, where the family vault. is-situated. The surpliced choir:and clergy of the private chapel at Arley fol- lowed the bier and sang. hymns all the way. About 12 or:13 members of the family and relatives fol= lowed ou foot, and there were ten carriages. Among thcsie present were (Monet and Mrs. Piers Egerton Warburton, the Earl of Lathom, the Hon. Mrs. Wil- braiiam, Sir Richard grooke,&c. The ceremony was attended by a congregation which completely filled the-church. The Rev. P.Slater, of St.James',Latch- ford, Warrington, represented the Warrington branch of the English Church Union, of which Mr. Warburton was president. There was a considerable attendance of clergy from the surrounding district.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

The Duke of Devonshire passed a quiet night on Wed- nesday. His condition remains much the same. Lord Walter Gordon Lennox, who has been appointed treasurer of the Queen's household, was on Wednesday re-elected for South-West Sussex without opposition. Chief Steward Heismeir, of the German Lloyd's steamer Ems, died at Southampton, on Thursd y. He was cleaning a revolver on Sunday, when the weapon exploded, and fatally wounded him in the stomach. The action in.which Mr. Henry Hansard claimed over £lB,OOO from the Hansard Union being the balance of the purchase money of plaintiff's printing business, was concluded on Thursday. The jury found for plain- tiff.

At the Shropshire Assizes, on Thursday, Thomas Griffiths was•sentenced to 20 years' penal servitude for the manslaughter of a man named John Peate, whom he stabbed at Ellesmere with a knife after Peate had struck him during a quarrel.

An alarniin; epidemic of measles is reported to have broken out, in the parish of Ruabon. 30 deaths occurred from the disease during the past month, and it has been found necessary to close the whole of the Board and National Schools in the district.

At an inquest at Stockport, on Thursday, a verdict of Wilful.murder "was returned against James Sharkey, a cotton operative, for kicking to death Catherine Bunt, aged thirty-nine, with whom he had lived with for 24 years. Prisoner,who had previously' illtreated the woman admitted the crime.

According to the Berlin "Medical Review," over 40,000 ceses of influenza have been reported in Berlin,. during the present outbreak, which, it is said, differs from the former onelin so far that it spreads more slowly. During the last eight days thirty deaths have occurred from the scourge, or from diseases. directly resulting from it. In Hamburg the disease has caused quite a panic; and last week the death-rate rose at one bound to 282 over the average. At the Canibridge Town Council, on Thursday, it was stated, in answer to Mr. Vinter, that Superinten- dent Innes' action in the production of the register oi prostitutes at the "pinning House" trial was autho- rised by the ternas of the charter. The Council decided by 23 votes against four to hold a, special meeting on December 18th4, with the view of arranging to promote a Bill in Parliament limiting or altogether abolishing the University's power. At Winchester Assizes, on Thursday, Fanny Ciane, aged 26,, domestic servant, lately employed at Barnes, near London, was sentenced to death for the murder of her newly-born child at Ventnor, wh.ereshe was stopping with her employer's family. • The girl admitted making away with the child and hiding it in some bushes on Barnes Common, but, after sentence had been passed, she shrieked and fell into a fit, and subsequently denied that sbe had killed' the child.

THE LAW OF EXCLUDED MIDDLE,

Sir,—As some of my remarks before the Penketh Mutual Improvement Association were much misunder- stood, may I ask you to insert this explanation ? From the above mentioned law I deduce this axiom :—Of two opposite and contradictory statements, if one be true, the other must needs be untrue. Now all our" know- ledge " shows early man as savage or semi-human—the uses of rude flint implethents—vide, M. Joli—" Man be- fore metals"—Lubbock's " Pre-historic times." This is one statement. The pulpit statement is just the con- trary of this. Here we have man created—perfect phy- sically and intellectually—and showing subsequent deterioration. Now of these two statements one can only be true—which ? One is a statement without physical evidence ; the other a statement from physical evidence. But the tradition is preached at the expense of its truth. In charity we must conclude that none of the preachers of the tradition see it as an untruth ; a view more credit- able to their hearts than their heads.—! am, &c. JOHN PEERS.

div.head: LIFEBOAT SATURDAY AND SUNDAY.
div.p: LIFEBOAT SATURDAY AND SUNDAY.

Sir,—At a meeting of the Manchester and Salford Life- boat Saturday Council and Executive Committee held in the Mayor's parlour, the other day, Alderman T. Bosdin Leech, Mayor of Manchester, who presided, ex- pressed the hope that this movement, which has been so successfully inaugurated in an inland centre would be energetically taken up in all the cities and towns throughout the country. £5,454 is the amount raised by this effort, which represents nearly twopence a head of the entire population of Manchester and ,Salford. Stockport has since followed and has raised a consider- able sum :—Belton is having a Lifeboat Saturday on December sth. Oldham also is now moving, and that energetic town I have no doubt will be well to the fore. Sir W. B. Forwood and a number of influential gentle- men waited upon the Mayor of Liyerpoel on Friday last asking his approval of a public meeting being called for the purpose of inaugurating a Lifeboat Sunday; that was decided to be convened on December 9th and I am certain that the first Seaport of the country will show an example worthy of its position. All this, coupled with the splendid result of the special appeal made a short time ago by the" Yorkshire Post," which realised over £3,500, must be very encouraging to the Com- mittee of Management, and as one of the firs: evidences of this, they have decides to increase the pay of the gallant Lifeboatmen to half asmuch again as they have been receiving, both for practice and service during the two winter quarters, when the hardships they have to endure are the greatest. Twopence per head of the population of the greatest maritime nation of the world, most people would consider a very modest sum to pay for the support ofothis great organisation for the saving of life at sea. I think those who have read the recent thrilling narra- tives of gallant rescues, as well as the adverse criticisms on account of a few unfortunate occrrences which how- ever are very rare, will be surprised to know that instead of twopence, less than a farthing per head is all the British nation contributed last year to the support of this life-saving fleet, and that for two-thirds of the cost of running it, the Committee had to fall back on the posthumous generosity of a few hundred, people, who have over a long term of years left money to this noble Institution. This I think, all will admit is a most pre-

KR. 11. WADE-DEACON'S CANDIDATURE. Under the auspices of Widnes Division Liberal Association, a public meeting of Liberals was held on Wednesday night, in Mr. Daintlth's Wirework, Halebank. Although the weather was very wet and stormy, there was a good audience, the room being well filled. In the absence of qr. W. Clarke, through illness; Mr. E.Carey occupied the chair,and on the platform were Major Waring, Messrs. H. A. James (of the Eighty Club, London), H. Wade-Dea- con, J.P. (Liberal candidate for the Division).— Knowles, and H. B. Shores (secretary). The Chair- man expressed regret at the absence of Mr. Clarke, and of the cause of it. Referring to Mr. Deacon, he assured the audience that the more they knew him and the more they would feel that he was the can- didate for their purpose at the next General Elec- tion.—Mr. H. A. James proposed the following re- solution :—" That this meeting expre.ises its un- abated confidence in the leadership of the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, M.P., and records its earnest hope that he may be permitted life and health to complete the great work he has undertaken—that of granting Home Rule to Ireland."—Major Waring seconded the motion,and alluded to the enthusiasm and confidence felt in Mr. Deacon's candidature.

Mr. Deacon who had an enthusiastic reception, said ever since their great defeat in 1886 the Liberals had been steadily progessing all over the country Still they had a very hard fight before them. They had a majority of 796 to pull down, and convert in- to a minority. The Liberals had one great thing to their advantage, and that was that they had one great cause to work for—Home Rule for Ireland. (Cheers.) They had also the advantage of the leadership of that great man,Mr. Gladstone. (Cheers) The Newcastle programme had been splendidly abused by the Tory party. Lord Hartington had said that the promises of Mr. Gladstone were not to be relied upon, but he (Mr. Deacon) would like to know whether the Unionists had fulfilled all their pledges ?. He thought they had not. The Local Gov- ernment Bill passed by the Conservatives, was based on Liberal principles, but it was faulty in one res- pect—it did not give full power to the popular local bodies, but had restricted and hampered them. and these restrictions would have to be removed here- after. Referring to the Technical Instruction Act, he said it was a good one, but no Tories, he thought could be proud of the means by which the end was obtained. Dealing with the licensing question, he said there were too many, public-houses almost everywhere. He believed that no measure would he acceptable which did not grant to each locality the right to make their own licensing law. (Ap- plause.) The resolution was put to the meeting and carried unanimously.
PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT THE TRAINING COLLEGE.

Yesterday afternoon the annual distribution of prizes to the students at the Warrington Training College took place, before a good attendance of parents and friends. The Rev. Canon Maclure, Dean of Manchester, presided, and there were also present —the Rev. Morley Stevenson (principal of the College), Canon Diggla, of Liverpool, Arch- deacon Barber (Chester), Rev. Canon Blundell, Rev. ,Uanon Penrbyn, Rev. F. S. Hop wuod, the Rector of Warrington -(the Rev. F. W. Willis), Rev. J. H. Stanning, Dr. Watkins, &c. The CHAIRMAN regretted that Lord Cross was unable to be present to distribute the prizes, as had been announced._ _ .

The Rev. Morley Stevenson spoke upon the work of the students. The results reflected the greatest credit upon the students and upQn his staff of fellow teachers, of whom he was proud and of whom he could speak with gratitude. Canon DIGGLE, in presenting the prizes,said that every credit was due to Mr. Stevenson, who had raised the Col- lege to the first rank in the country, with the assistance of his colleagues and the efforts of the students. He complimented the college on holding the first position in the country for needle-work. He stated that the aver- age cost at the Warrington Training College, was £42 19s. 4d. per annum, which spoke much for the excel- lence of the administration, whilst the cheerful and happy appearance of the students showed that they were not starved. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Archdeacon BARBER proposed a vote of thanks to Canon Diggle for presenting the prizes, Canon MacClure for presiding, and the Rev. Morley Stevenson and the association teachers for their work during the past year. The Rev. F. W. Wittas seconded the motion, which was carried. . .

During the afternoon part songs were given in a creditable manner by the senior and junior students, and after the meeting the visitors and students were entertained to tea. carious position for a society with such a beneficient pur- pose to be in. Most of the criticisms I have read display considerable ignorance both of its financial posi- tion, and as to how it is inaugurated, consequently all kinds of impracticable or injudicious proposals are suggested as example that it ought to be under Govern- ment control. If such critics could only realize that their communications and utterances may be the means of valuable lives being sacrificed they would get fuller information before ventilatint, opinions that are calcu- lated to do no good, but on the contrary much harm. Interference on the part of the Government might be the means of disorganising a noble volunteer force, for I think the public ought never to lose sight of the fact that the service is in spirit and in practice an entinly voluntary one, and that the heroism which marks it is distinctly traceable to these conditions. Those who have an intimate knowledge of fishermen are well aware that although they may be poor, they are from the nature of their occupatien perhaps as inde- pendent a body of men as can be found anywhere. They may be led to do or dare anything, but they cannot be driven, and moreover their daily occupation gives their, not only an intimate knowledge of the handling of boats, but also of the numerous hidden dangers that abound on almost every part of our treacherous coast, a knowledge which can only be gained by daily experience. What is wanted is less criticism and more money. Al- though I quite uphold a prompt and thorough investiga- tion of any irregularities,and I strongly object to the great publicity that is givea to the few failures that are bound from time to time to occur through want of tact on the part of an honorary official or an injudicious act of cox- swain in a moment of difficulty; either of these might easily bring about what has recently taken place at one or two stations. I firmly believe that the chief difficulties in connection with this great life-saving service would disappear, if the public contributed rn,ire liberally to its support, which is an absolute necessity if its arrange- ments are to be perfect. The Lifeboat Saturday and Sunday appears to me to be the best plan of giving- all classes of the community an opportunity of contributing according to their ability. Let a few earnest workers in each town make up their minds to carry this out, and juding from my own ex- perience, the results will be eminently satisfactory.—l am, yours truly, CHARLES W. MACARC. Chairman of the Executive Committee of the Man- chester and Salford Lifeboat Saturday Fund. Westbourne, St. Annes-on-the-Sea.

ENTERTAINMENT AT TUE CONSEILVATIVE CLUB. On Thursday evening, an entertainment was given in the Conservative Club. by Professor J. L. Yv yman. This was Professor Wyman's first appear- ance in Penketh, and the announcement of his visit attracted a good audience. The programme consisted of conjuring tricks, ventriloquism, shadow illusions, &e. Professor Wyman's performances were much appreciated, the shadowgraphy in par- ticular eliciting much applause. Mr. 11. C. Hope, from the Royal Aquarium, presided at the piano in an able manner.

div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery Office on Wednesday. Mr. 11. Coleburn presided, and there were present Messrs. W. Mellor, W. Littler, W. Whittaker, W. F. Salkeld (secretary). The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £l7 13s. and interest fall- ing due amounting to .£25 83.3 d.; and also to pay off the Lily ot the Valley G.U.O. Oddfellows the mortgage of £2OO. The minutes were passed, on the motion of Mr. Mellor, seconded by Mr. Littler.—The Secretary read the following letter he had received from Mr. E. Marshall, secretary of the Board of Commissioners understand that Mr. Barker has informed you that your proportion in respect of the making of Victoria-road will be about £5OO. May I venture to suggest that you take steps to obtain this sum. We should deem it a favour if you could re-imburse early in the new year, other- wise we shall be seriously hampered for funds before the close of our financial year."—Mr.. Mel- lor moved that the secretary reply that the subject was receiving the consideration of the Board and at the same time ask for particulars of the apportionments.— The motion was seconded and carried.—The Secretary said the lower field of the Cemetery would have been worse had not the sewer been placed in the road. This drain was of very great magnitude, going through the big pool and under the Ship Canal. This information could be given to the ratepayers at a meeting which would have to be held before the money required could be paid.
THE PROPOSED VEHICULAR BRIDGE ACROSS THE MERSEY.

Acting on the recommendation of the General Purposes Committee, the Widnes Local;Board on Tuesday approved of a joint memorial from the local authorities of Widnes and Runcorn in favour a new bridge across tbe Mersey and ordered the seal of the Board to be affixed and the memorial duly presented to the County Councils of Lanca- shire and Cheshire. The pPtition sets forth "that the area of Widnes is 3,039, the population 30,011, and the rateable value £139,339; whilst the area of Runcorn is 1,153, the population over 20,000. and the rateable value ..£56,000. The distance between the counties of Lancaster and Chester, measuring across the estuary from Widnes to Runcorn, is 1,300 feet, which distance is spanned by a railway an foot bridge belonging to the London and North-Western Railway Company, erected in the year 1868. The distance by road between Widnes and Runcorn through Warrington, is about 14i miles in length, and very circuitous. No bridge, it is pointed out,other than the footbridge referred to, exists over the Mersey between Warrington on the one hand and the sea on the other, a distance of 24 miles, and, with the exception of an obsolete ferry at Widnes, there are at the present time no direct means of transporting goods and merchan- dise by road from one side of the estuary to the other in consequence of which large numbers of the inhabitants of both counties are occasioned great loss and inconvenience. The memorialists are strongly of opinion that the diffi- culty of access between the counties was most pre- judicial to the interests of the inhabitants, and that if suitable communication existed the traffic between the counties would largely increase. Tney are further of opinion that the difficulty complained of can be overcome by the construction of a bridge suitable for vehicular traffic across the estuary of the Mersey near to the present railway bridge, and that such a bridge would be of great advantage not only to the towns represented by the memorialists, but also to the whole of the mid, and greater part of West, Cheshire on the one hand, and to the large and industrial district of South-west Lanca- shire on the other. The petitioners are advised, upon eminent authority, that a suitable structure of sufficient capacity and strength can be erected at the point named for the cotnparatively moderate expenditure of about £140,000. They think that, by the collection of a reasonable toll upon vehicular and pedestrian traffic a sufficient revenue might be obtained to cover the cost of construction and main- tenance and:point out further that a new bridge would place Widnes and South-west Lancashire in direct communication with the Manchester Ship Canal, and the extensive docks connected with that undertaking at Runcorn and Weston Point. Under these circumstances, they ask the county councils of the respective counties to take the matter into their immediate consideration.

HOW THE CLERGY AND LAITY MAY BEST EBBE IN TOUCH. Mr. James White introduced a discussian on this sub- ject. He argued that this might be brought about by making the services more interesting and as simple as it was possible to make them. He was in favour of shorter sermons, and stated that one half of the clergy did not i take advantage of the opportunities of getting n touch• with the people afforded by visiting themat their homes."' He advocated the election of Church Councils in every parish, with the Vicar as Chairman, who ought always to respect the opinion of the laity.—Mr. C. S. Burgess also spoke strongly in favour of visiting,and advocated the formation of a Church party to defend the Church against disestablishment.—Mr. Stokes and Mr. Mellor also dwelt upon the apathy of the clergy to visiting—Mr. Hankinson observed that it would be an advantage if there was a better feeling amongst the laity than exisetd at the present time.—His Lordship, in summing up the discussion, said while admitting that there were a great many weaknesses in the harness of the clergy it was a great mistake to overestimate the weak side of things. The clergy were continually endeavouring to draw the laity closer to them but as to how they could be more success- ful in their efforts the speakers had not suggested one single line of action beyond what had already been tried. The great thing to do was to use the old custom with new vigour and sympathise with one another. The laity had certain responsibilities, and the initiative should not always be left to come from the clergy. He- was in favour of the service being made as attractive as possible, but did not think it advisable that the sermons should be snort as though they were something they were ashamed of. He believed that substantial pro- gress was being made in the right direction, and that it was not greater was not due to lack of earnestness on the part of the clergy.—On the proposition of the Rev. H. B. Blogg,seconded by Mr. Hankinson, a vote of con- dolence with Canon Greenall in his illness was passed, and the proceedings terminated with the Benediction.

Earl Spencer and Mr. John Morley were the principal speakers at a dinner given at the Eighty Club, on Wed- nesday evening, to Dr. Spence Watson. Lord Spencer denied that the Liberals were putting Home Rule in the background. None of them, he said, believed that the constituencies in the country were tired of Home\ Rule.

div.head: VIOLENT GALE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: VIOLENT GALE AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday night a gale of great force and in- tensity broke over Runcorn. The wind swept along with verrifie powe4. and at intervals there were storms ofiiain and: hallStonea,. the latter of exeen- tional size.. Fortunately no very serious damage is reported. In almost every street in. Runcorn broken slates and chimney pots strew the way, and in several instances the chimneys-have been bodily blown down. lb, Trentham-street the vielemee of the gale made the houses' rock, and some of the inhabitants did not retire to rest lest in their sleep the buildings should tumble- about their ears. A passenger by. the last train: from Liverpool des- cribed Runcorn Bridge as- swinging before the pressure of the furious blasts, and it was impassable for foot passengers. At Mr. Davenport's-, in Duke's Field,the chimney crashed throughthe roof into,the room below, and at Mr. the tripe dresser'S, the chimney was thrown through the skylight on to the staircase, smash- ing the balustrade. A. quantity of bricks also fell down the sittine, room chimney, and covered the furniture with soot and dust. Mr. and Mrs. Allen had a narrow escape from being struck by the falling bricks. In Greenway-road two houses in course of erection by Messra. Farrell. for Mr. James Ditchfield. were partly blown down, the whole of one side- of the buildings being demolished. The loss to those concerned will ne very heavy. At Old Quay the Alum Works, which are partly corke.txucted of wood, have been somewhat damaged, but not sotriient to hinder the process of manufacture.

Yesterday morning the gale had somewhat al:Med in violence, but hail and snow felt in large quantities, accompanied by thunder and lightning. After dinner the wind moderated to its normal condition, and for a time the sun shone. The shipping at th docks escaped damage.

The gale was also experienced with all its severity in Widnes; broken chimney pots and slates are in evidence in all the roads. Nothing of a seriou&nature has occurred. At Ditton a straw rick was bbDwn over, at Taylor's farm, and scattered, and part of the greenhouse was demolished. LOSS OF LIFE AND GREAT DAMAGE IN THE COUNTRY.

Telegrams received from different parka of the country show that a severe southwest gale raged on Wednesday night. At Windsor Great Park much damage has been done to fine elms and oaks. LIFEBOATS, AT' WORM •

There was a heavy storm in, the Bristol Channel on Wednesday ni;.7,ht,..and severalf casualities are reported. The iron ship Dunbleir, belonging to Gillison and Chad- wick, Liverpool, dragged its anchors off Barry and went ashoreon the rocks. A. tug boat took 14 of the crew ashore. The remainder, la in number, are still on board: Penarth4 lifeboat was towed out to the Dim- blair,. and succeeded in taking off the remainder oi the crew, including Captain Golding.

_ FALL OF A, CHIMNEY A PUBLICAN KILLED. About two o'Clock on Thursday morning, during the prevalence of the great storm,.the roof, chimney, &c., of the Horse Shoe.lnn, Dorrington, near Shrewsbury, was blown down, And the la ndlbrd John Hotchkiss, together with his wife,..who were in bed at the time, were buried in the debris. When the body of the. man was recovered it was found that he was quite dead, and although life was not extinct in the woman, but little hope is held out for her recovery.

LOSS OF A FRENCH, BARCRIE: AND ALL HANDS, At Swansea the French- barque Lenore parted her anchor and drove across the thebay. She was visible from Mumbles Lighthouse, but noone could render assis- tance. She drove before the storm on the opposite coast at Brighton Ferry,,where she lies a total wrecks She had a crew of twelve hands,, and belonged to Nantes, All the CLVAR are. beNeved to be lost. One body was washed ashore at Briton Ferry. It is now beyond doubt that the Crew of the Frenc:x Barque Zenore,. wrecked on Thursday night in Swansea Bay, were all drowned.

At Butlington the Severn has overflowed, covering miles of country„ and the whole of tho. Severn valley ia flooded more or leas disastrously. Serious floods are also reported in the valley of the Dovey, and in the Carnarvonshire wed Merionethshire valleys.

Tha Channel passages bt.tween Dover and the Continent, on Thursday night, wsre the roughest ever made. The Ostend boat was usable to leave. Ostend, owing to the fearful sea. Gtt Tong, near Bolton, on Thursday night,. during the gale a mineral water manufactszy was blown down.
A man named Thomas Rigby was arrested at Sheffield on Tuesday on a charge of having kicked to death a woman named Herbeit. _ -
Henry Atherton, a collier, belonging to Ince-in-Maker- fieid, was at the Liverpool assizes on Wednesday found guilty of the manslaughter of his wife, and sentenced to penal servitude for 20 years.

div.head: MEETING AT WARRINGTOS.
div.p: MEETING AT WARRINGTOS.

On Wednesday evening a largely attended and ' influential meeting was held in the Town Hall, Warrington for the purpose of hearing as address from the Rev. Benjamin Waugh,. honorary director of the National Society for the Prevention al Cruelty to Children,. on the work of the Society, and to con- sider the advisability of forming an Aid Committee of the Society for Warrington. The meeting had been convened by the Mayor (Alderman E.Greenall) who presided. Amongst those present were—the Rector (Rev. F. W. Willis), Rev. J. Yonge, Rev. F: Freeston, Rev. E. O..Es Carleton, Rev. F. Slater, Mr:. L. Voisey, Councillor Shaw Green, Fsev. Fathet Feeney, Mr. R. Garnett,. Rev. J. J. Langliarn, Rev. A.. , Freeman, Rev. J. Gunnell, Alderman Wright,'J. T. Ridgway, Captain Buckton, Rev. L. J. T. Darwell, !Mr. 11. Broadbent, Rev. J. G. Richards,. Mr. John Fairclongh, Dr. S. Smith,. Rev. T. Ross, Itlr. A. H. Los, Rev. Mr. Cook,. Rey. H. V. Pigott). Mr. R. E. Garnett, &c. Letters of apology for nen-attendance were read from Ml. .L C. Parr, Mr. Z. Aernitage, and Mr. W. Len. The MAIVOR expressed his pleasure at seeing so large and repre.4eratative a meetinge He had, as Mayor, been requested to call that meeting together, and it was with the greatest pleasure he consented to do so. (Applause.) He should like it to be undeastood that the object of that. meeting was to discuss whether it was consiaered advis- able by those present to form an aid committee insthis towns. andthat up to then fleshing definite had been settled and no one was pledged to anything. He was anxious- tofinci out from the sense a that meeting,. if the scheme would be supported b'y, the town. One of the letters he. had received was fromGanon Heron who wrote that 'although, unable to be presenthe was with them in suirit ;And lee had letters also from Chief Constable' Hunt and tite-sehool inspector, Aft... Riley, both of whorrn said that if the aed committee was formed they wouldi do all in thein power to assist the officers of the society. (Hear, hearrand applause). The Rev. R. W4ttiGH,VlllO was reeeived with applause, said they were there on a platform, which was non- ' political and non-sectarian. (Hewed. hear.) The tend- ency of civilisation, was, he said, decidedly to produce crueltrte childten. Where humanity was simple and natural,,. and amongst savage tribes„ there was less cruelty to children than amongst civilised people, and this arose.from the fact that among savages if they did not wane a child they could destroy 'lb at once, while they whe.were- crrilised hanged people who did that. Therefore,. civiliestson drove to expedients and those expedients.were the cause of the long-suffering of thou- sands of children. Could people in England do as the Chinese and the Riede() on the Ganges did—put away a child beethe pain of a few moments, then they should be 'saved ftom that Society,which at present bad to deal with the-putting away of children byeleng-protracted cruelty. The cruelties discovered by his agents were In the villages amongst a rural population as they were in towns amongst a manufacturing population. He should say, that the condition which chieffy produced it was self-indulgence„ whether at the village-public-house or at the billiard room of the towns. Its did not exist because of large families. In 2,000 caseseirt which they prosecuted the average number of children in a family was 2-43. The families were small hecauseparents would , not let theirs children live. Tracing back the history of a, few selected eases he discovered that were but two child- ren did live there had, been six or seven bern. Further, analysing, he came to the conclusion that many were making a profit out of the death of theirohitdren. They had insured in, England 1.500,000 children:be-hinging to all classes, respectable and non-respectablwanaongst the working .people„by people who were sober and by people who pawned eyerything week after week._ Alluding to the large number of children put out to nurse mostly to baby fermi he-said he spent £4OO in answering adver- tisements.for children to adopt. A woman announced herself aemarried seven years and anxious to adopt a child. He repliedto the advertisement saying he had a child to put out,. and an answer was received containing proposals' for negotiation. His agent went to the woman and coming straight to the point, said, with a confiden- tial look, !.4-Can you eet rid of it ? " The woman replied, "Well; what for The woman said hen terms were £so,but the agent represented that the medier was poor and was anxious to,be rid of the child, and, the woman at length agreed tote he £25 with the child ,and £25 when she brought the death certificate. Since that took place they had discovered scores of such people, and they had just landed' one woman. 10 years penal senvitude. On that woman'e preraises.there were many disesed garments of linOishbabies, but they could only prosecute for one single child. In another case they had traced 28 babies to one woman in three months, and not one of them 'could she account for. In one year be had tabulated 15,200. advertisements likeethose he had referred to in the London papers alone. It had been nobody'slausiness in this country to look up.those dread- ful slaughter-houses which were being estabiisheti every- where ancl, were making £l5O and £2OO &year for vile women. There was no record in England of the children born and-not allowed to live, and no machinery to tell` how many- were smuggled in small boxes, to their last ieeting place. When the story did come out they -ilithilereaet need tn send missionaries to foreign countries. He knew a. few things already but they could not be made publin yet.. There was no doubt an enormous in- crease amongst the better class of artisans of still-born children. Bating into the very life of England was the 'anti-population theory, and side by side with it was the growth ,of materialism amongst the masses. Mr. Waugh then expleined the methods of working of the Socieey.He said that when an aid Committee was formed they asked it to guarantee a minimum of £l5O a year, and the society would then guarantee that the treasurer was never without money so long as it was spent In protecting children. They started 20 new committees every-yearand they cost them at least £2,500 more than they pare theme In the second and third year they be- gan to pay theinway, and in the fourth year they began to contribute to. the central fund. Me: Waugh then gave various details of the work of the Society, and was loudly applauded on taking his seat. Questions having been invited, Mr. Waugh, in answer to the Rev. B. (11. E. Carleton' said that they aimed at eachdistrict comprising about 100,000) people as one officer could manage about that number. The,Rscalate expressed his strong sympathy with the Society, and said he believed there were many cases of shameful neglect of children in Warrington. A man at the heck of the room having mentioned that he wasconnected with the insurance business, asked what number of cases of cruelty were attributable to children being insured, and also how.many murders gad been committed to get insurance money. The Rev. B. Weevil said the reason, why he had not touched upon insurance horrors, was that he had only ' that night todo with the machinery and show how it ,would work.. If the Committee weroJorroed in Warringt. ton and hewere there at the end of 22 raonths he should; tell.theneof a few cases in that district. In a speech the- previous day Mr. Chamberlain had- called attention to, 113 cases of, cruelty to children wha.were insured in his ' own town in OW year. Last year-the. society had 10)1 cases of, cruelty to children who were insured for the total sum of pretty nearly £6.,0Q: As to how many cases of murder had been attributable-to insurance, the difference between the cases detected and the cases =- detected was each that he could not answer. If it were meant by murder letting child rertielie•for insurance medley, he, should say they had been very mech more numeroue than people in England believed: He did not makenny charge against the great bodyv of working-men., boat against, theualleus brutes who.loved beer and did, not care-for. a baby. The ordinaeye rue. of workinkpeople loved theirehildren as mucheaai anybody else .in the country. (Meer, hear.) The same man who had eti.it the question then read aorae denunciation of Mr. Waugh.. which had appeared in, the "-Agents' Journal."' At the same time., he ex- pressed himself satisfied with theanswer, and hoped the • movement that was being, inaugurated wosild be a success.
The Rev. Father FuEnnx.spoke in favour ot the pro- motion, of a branch of the Society in Warrington. as did also the Revs. J. Yonge,.E. K. Freeston, anal. Gunnell.

Dr-. R. SMITH moved "-That, in view of the beneficial effetts of the operation.of, the National Soniety for the Prevention of Cruel to, Children in London and many other parts of,, the Kingdom' iti hereby re- solved that an aid sof' that Society be established in Warrington and distrNt." The RECTOR seconded, and Mr. A. H. Linn supported, this proposal which:was adopted unanimously. It was then proposed by Captain granreti, seconded. by Councillor 51a,..4w GREEN, and carried :--" That the, following ladies and gentlemen forum the General Coin, mittee, with power to add to their number, to appoint an executive, and to communicate. with the Central ' Committee for- incorporation :—Mrs. Slater, Rev.,. F. Slater, the Rector, s. Willis, Mr: W. Sharp, Mrs. R. Garnett, MissMilner (Moore), Mrz,J',. D. Buckton,, Miss Pierpoint, the. Mayoress, Miss Duny,Rev. E. C. E. Carle- ton, Mrs. Carleton, Mrs. Crosfieldy, Mrs. Harrison,„ Miss B. Dutton, Mrs. Parr, Mrs. Lyon. Mrs. Lee, 111 m Isaac, Mrs. Leigh, Wilson, Mrs. James. Fairclough, Mr; James Fairclough, Mrs. Sherratt, Mrs., Pigot, Rev. H. V. Pigot, Mrs. J. Cherley, Mrs. Vere Davies., Mrs. Broadbent, Mr. Broadbent, Mrs. McGregor, Mrs. H. Woods, Mr. Apple- ton, Miss Harvey, Rev. Father Feeny, Rev. J. Yonge, Rev., F. E. Freeston. Rev.. J. Gunnell, Mr. J. C. Parr, Mr., John Crosfield, Mk. Ziba Armitage, Mrs. W. C. Jonas, Mrs. Captain Royse, Rev. L. J. T, Darwall, Mr. 4.. H. Fleming, and Mk. J. Shaw Green. „ Votes of thanks to, Mr. Waugh and the Mayor closed the proceedings.

• •r 4 • • - BOROUGH OF ,E , WARRINGTON. ~-.._•;t4k. • THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS). 1. ACTS, 1878 to 1890. THE RABIES (MUZZLING OF DOGS) ORDER, 1889. In consequence ofthe increase of RABIES in Lancashire,the Board of Agriculture have directed that the Compulsory Muzzling Regulations shall be more stringently administered by the various Local Authorities. NOTICE IS THEREFORE HEREBY GIVEN "That no dog shall be allowed to be in or on any public place unless such dog is muzzled with a muzzle so constructed as to ren- der it impossible for such dog while wearing the same to bite any person or animal, but not so as to prevent suchdog from breathing ' reely or lapping water." " If any dog is found in or on any public place without be- ing muzzled as aforesaid, the person for the time being in charge of the dog and the owner thereof and the person allow- ing the same to be in or on such public place, shall be guilty of an offence against the Act of 1878." Any offence against the above Order subjects the offender to a penalty of £2O. All stray dogs and all dogs not muzzled as aforesaid will be seized and slaughtered or otherwise dealt with as pro- vided by the Order. Dated this Eleventh Day of December, 1891. J. LYON WHITTLE, Town Clerk. Town Hall. Warrington.
